subsubtopic: CANCELLATION OF SERVICES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada has been made well aware of the feelings of the people of Canada regarding VIA Rail cuts, and cutbacks in passenger service. A 19 per cent cutback of service in Canada means that 50 per cent of the service in western Canada is cut back, almost 50 per cent of the service in Atlantic Canada will disappear, and 1,600 VIA lay-offs will have an effect on 8,000 jobs in Canada. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski):
That this House instruct the Minister of Transport to rescind immediately the order in council cancelling one fifth of Canada's rail passenger service and call public hearings so that he may be informed of the current facts and the absolute need for this service in all regions of Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the VIA cutbacks which have upset Canadians from coast to coast. In view of the September 28 decision of the Canadian Transport Commission which said that the accounting system used to estimate financial losses of passenger trains is inadequate and should be reviewed, and since this means that the decision of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to cut VIA services is based on completely outdated and inaccurate information, a fact which was confirmed by direct information given to me recently in Moncton and Saint John, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis):
That this House urge the government to rescind the order in council abandoning passenger service, at least until the Canadian Transport Commission or the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport holds a full public inquiry.

That this House condemn the Minister of Transport for his now infamous dictatorial edict of July 27 which removed all rail passenger service from many of these rural communities in Manitoba, leaving several of them totally isolated.

That the House instruct the government to postpone any cuts to passenger rail service until the democratic process embodied in the Canadian Transport Commission has been satisfied and public hearings are held to determine the fate of these lines.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the widespread demonstrations last weekend protesting the build-up of nuclear arms by both the superpowers, and in view of the decision taken by the United States to construct neutron bombs which are conceived to destroy humanity while preserving property, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That this House go on record calling for nuclear disarmament in Europe and throughout the world, and that there be an immediate ban on neutron weapons and an early move to East-West talks on arms control. Further, that this House and every member present have a vital and responsible role to play in bringing the world back from the brink of nuclear holocaust where we stand today.
This is a motion in support of global nuclear disarmament. Surely that is what this House and nation stand for.

speechtext:

In a front page headline the Saint John Telegraph-Journal on August 27 referred to the proposed "Atlantic" and other cancellations in New Brunswick as "Ottawa cutting the heart out of New Brunswick". Since the cancellation falls hardest on areas where no affordable or convenient alternative passenger service exists, and on those who cannot afford a more expensive means of travel, I therefore move under the terms of Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett):
That the government do now immediately revoke the order in council cancelling certain VIA passenger service, renegotiate more for favourable VIA contracts with the railroads, and in general establish a VIA service which meets the needs as expressed by provincial governments, unions, chambers of commerce, mayors, university student bodies and a multitude of others.

subsubtopic: REASONS FOR MINISTER'S ACTION IN AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS IN SERVICE
speechtext:
My question, Madam Speaker, is directed to the Minister of Transport. In the House of Commons last Thursday the Minister of Transport informed members of the House that he had a first version of a VIA Rail Act. He also confirmed earlier in that day during Question Period that he was reviewing, and would amend, the

October 26, 1981
Oral Questions
infamous costing order R63-13. Since the lack of a proper legislative mandate, and an outdated and unfair costing order are central to the difficulties which plague VIA Rail, and since the decision to cut back VIA Rail services by 20 per cent emanates from this inadequate structure, may I ask the minister why he is so insistent on forging ahead with the cutbacks before these matters are put in order, particularly, Madam Speaker, since the propriety of the minister's actions is clearly brought into question both inside and outside this chamber?

subsubtopic: REASONS FOR MINISTER'S ACTION IN AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS IN SERVICE
speechtext:
I believe, and the government believes, for budgetary reasons and reasons of transportation policy, that the reduction of routes is essential. The discussion of the quality of costing order R63-13, and a discussion on the possibility and desirability of a bill on VIA are two other objectives which are not really related to the operation which now needs to be done, and which will give VIA the possibility of doing a good job. This necessitates the elimination of some routes. The way some members were talking you would have thought it was the reverse situation, that 80 per cent of the routes had been eliminated, as opposed to 20 per cent being eliminated and 80 per cent maintained.
There are a number of exaggerations around us this afternoon. It is regrettable and unfortunate. On the radio the other morning I heard, "Choo Choo, Choo, there won't be a train from Vancouver any more." This is not true at all. As a matter of fact, one of the transcontinentals is maintained.

Obviously the minister believes his actions are correct, but at the same time he chooses to ignore the CTC, and chooses to ignore the Parliament of Canada, and chooses to ignore the needs of Canadians. Why does the minister refuse to allow Parliament and the people of Canada to share in the formulation of a clear rail passenger policy before he arbitrarily orders the passenger service out of existence?
Is it true, Madam Speaker, that we may expect further cuts if this decision is allowed to go unchallenged? Is it true Canadians will experience further cutbacks next year? Is it true that the eastern and western arm of VIA Rail will probably be wiped out? Is it true that existing rolling stock is now being scrapped? Is it true that the LRC scheduled to go into service this week will not be going into service? Why does the minister refuse to debate this very important public policy item in Parliament so that parliamentarians and the people of Canada will have an opportunity of sharing in making the kind of policy that will meet the needs of the 1980s and on to the year 2000?
My hon. friend who, I always thought, would have been a progressive and a dynamic Minister of Transport-
He was.

-has been repeatedly trying to delay, first by saying it should be sent to the CTC, and then by saying it should be sent to a parliamentary committee, which I accepted at one point. He said it should be delayed until we have a VIA bill; it should be delayed until we have the extraordinary costing formula that would solve all problems for all time. This is an accumulation of delays which would lead to a situation where at one point, in the end, there might not be something to help. This is what we are trying to do. We are trying to help VIA. The management of VIA are fully in agreement with what we are doing.
No, they are not.

Of course they are. They wrote to my predecessor on the same subject. They gave my predecessor exactly the same recommendation as they gave me. That recommendation has been incorporated in the decision which we made on July 27. The hon. member knows that.
I do not accept that.
He could not make up his mind on the subject. That is something else.
Hear, hear!
How do you know what the recommendations to him were?
Well I can read the files, can I not?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. We will not get through several questions if we do not allow the minister to answer.

On the delay in the coming into activity of the LRCs-light, rapid and comfortable trains-my answer is very simple. The management have repeatedly expressed their satisfaction with these trains, but there have been the usual technical difficulties in matters of this kind. This is why they were located close to the manufacturer, so they could be sent back rather rapidly.
Oh, oh!
They have had problems. It will mean a delay of about four weeks altogether. It is expected that some of the ten trains will go back into activity before the end of the four weeks.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister. I do not know whether the minister has been asked this question in the House, but in terms of delay when was the decision made which was announced on July 27? How many days or weeks before the House adjourned? What was the reason for the delay in the minister's announcement?
October 26, 1981

Returning partly to the question of the hon. member for Vegreville, if the minister is so sure of his facts, what is wrong with having this matter referred to the CTC, the body which was structured under the National Transportation Act to hear these matters, so that one of the budgetary reasons which is being used by the minister now will not be again used under the costing formulae that no one understands? VIA Rail does not know what it is paying for its rental of the rails.

Madam Speaker, I have explained repeatedly why it was not being sent to the CTC. First of all one has to go to the law. Section 64(1) of the National Transportation Act indicates specifically that the government can act by order in council in these matters. That is legal. The reason for the law is simply that there will be occasions in the life of a railway system when what needs to be done is not a study of each route particularly, but a total rationalization exercise. This is why the law anticipated that particular necessity. This is why the law indicates that it can be done.
What would have happened is very simple. Mr. Lang tried it and failed because of circumstances which my hon. friend may have in mind. I would have had to go to the CTC and give a directive. I would have had to tell the CTC that there were limitations on the amounts of money that could be spent. Half a million bucks was about the level.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Half a billion.
Half a billion, of course.
Of course! What's half a billion!

I would have had to suggest to the CTC that it might consider maintaining one of the two transcontinental services. I would have had to tell the CTC that it would have to take into consideration the situation of isolated towns, cities and communities. I would have had to tell the CTC something it indicated on its own, that commuter services were a provincial responsibility. I would have had to say all that.
Why didn't you?
The same people who accuse me of being arbitrary now, would have said that I was twisting the arm of the CTC. This is why we have done it the way we have. We have done it directly.
Tear the arm right off the CTC.
In so doing, we have saved three or four years of time. We have saved the necessary money to give to VIA to buy itself proper equipment at this time.

subtopic: RAILWAYS' CONTRIBUTION TO GROWTH OF COUNTRY
RAILWAYS' CONTRIBUTION TO GROWTH OF COUNTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand the minister has some history with railways. His father worked in the railways. I must say that I do not
Oral Questions
think the minister is following in the same track as his father who had some identity with railways.
Does the minister not believe that at this particular time, when there is stress and strain in this country that the railways helped to bring together from coast to coast, when we are talking about the Charter of Rights and discussions and forums, it would have been a very positive thing if he could have laid down some abbreviated terms of reference for the CTC? If he had done that, this thing could have been discussed, argued and debated within an abbreviated time period, and the taxpayers, the mayors, and all those people who came here today, and officials from coast to coast, would know the one completely idiotic situation, that VIA Rail under the costing formula is the only railway that I know of in the world that cannot get an explanation of the bill that it is paying to CN and CP for the rental of its rails. That much at least could have been cleared up and, Madam Speaker, if it is not cleared up then the same type of costing formula will do just what the hon. member for Vegreville says it will do, and if that is so, then we might as well eliminate every passenger service.

subtopic: RAILWAYS' CONTRIBUTION TO GROWTH OF COUNTRY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is the problem I have had. My hon. friends on the other side, and some of them on all sides forget, when they think about it-

subtopic: RAILWAYS' CONTRIBUTION TO GROWTH OF COUNTRY
speechtext: Some on your side, too.

subtopic: RAILWAYS' CONTRIBUTION TO GROWTH OF COUNTRY
speechtext:
Yes, indeed. They forget that in your lifetime and in mine we have seen three revolutions; the revolution of the automobile, of the bus, and of the plane. We are now seeing the revolution of electronics. There is no way that railways could come through these four revolutions untouched.
What we are doing now is adjusting railway passengers transportation to contemporary times. That has to be done. It is being done in every part of the world now. I know it is painful, because we are all romantic about railways. I was born with railway smoke in my nose. We are all romantic about it, but when you tell people that half a billion dollars is going toward subsidizing rail passengers now, they do not know it. I thank the opposition very much for giving me the opportunity of reminding them of that. When they are told that, people say they agree with us that there must be limitations to the amount of money which can be dedicated to this particular mode of transportation.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no one on this side of the House and no Canadian outside the House who is being romantic about keeping passenger trains. All of us are sick and tired of the minister's philosophizing, when he does not know a damn thing about transportation.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS
speechtext: Four economists in the employ of the government, of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Transport, have said that this decision is, and I quote them, "-as uninformed and inconsistent an exercise in transportation planning as could be imagined." In light of the fact that the CTC and the government's own economists have said that VIA Rail is unjustifiably paying 60 per cent of its operating costs to Canadian Pacific and Canadian National, compared to the 25 per cent paid by Amtrak in United States, and since the order in council is based on out-of-date and misleading information, would the minister at least agree to delay the implementation of the order in council until either the CTC or the parliamentary committee on transportation have held a full public hearing on the matter?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have said before that we will not delay implementation so I am not going to repeat it. The only thing that could convince us to delay would be a court action, which I understand is being taken today, or was taken last Friday. Of course if that comes about and if there is an injunction to prevent implementation of the order in council, we will obey the law.
All through these days I have heard from the hon. member for Regina West and from Transport 2000 that they are not opposed to some reduction of services. The hon. member said the other day in debate in the House:
We are not trying to justify the retention of all 21 routes, but I submit that at least half of them are viable.
The member is quite in agreement with the principle that one has to rationalize railways, and the debate between himself and ourselves relates to how many routes should be terminated and how many routes should be reduced. That is a debate which is quite normal, but the principle is accepted by everyone. It is a matter of disagreement as to the number of cutbacks which should take place.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING CUTBACKS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I know the minister wants to be fair. If one looks at my opening paragraph or two, I said that we wanted the government to rescind the order, but we agreed with the motion of the official opposition that, to be reasonable, we should at least ask for a delay, and the minister knows that.

subtopic: OPERATION OF BUS ROUTES PURSUANT TO CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION ORDER
OPERATION OF BUS ROUTES PURSUANT TO CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION ORDER
speechtext:
I have a second question for the minister. In the wild rush of the minister, of the President of the Treasury Board and the cabinet, thinking they were going to save $100 million by the order in council, is it correct that in the order in council ordering the cancellation of these routes, the government forgot about all the bus routes that the Canadian Transport Commission ordered VIA Rail to
run, such as the routes from Fredericton to Moncton and from Prince Albert to Saskatoon? The order in council takes effect November 15. Will these buses still keep running to connect with trains that the government has already cancelled? I would like to ask the minister if he would explain that to us, and would he go back to the drawing board and check his homework?

subtopic: OPERATION OF BUS ROUTES PURSUANT TO CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION ORDER
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will obviously do that.

subtopic: OPERATION OF BUS ROUTES PURSUANT TO CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION ORDER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: The order in council varies a number of decisions the CTC has previously taken. I do not know where buses come into that, but obviously that was not the main objective.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the revised seventh report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, presented to the House on Wednesday, June 17, 1981, be concurred in.
He said: Madam Speaker, you will remember, because you were in chair on Thursday, that my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and I put questions relating
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
to House business to the government House leader. At that time we sought the assurance of the government House leader that if I were to follow the instructions of my committee, the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, and ask for concurrence of the House in our revised seventh report today, there would be a full and proper debate on that committee report, that we would have a chance to have a full discussion and that no action would be taken by the government to prevent that discussion from taking place.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, that earlier this summer when I moved concurrence in July in the fourth report of the standing committee, the government took the extraordinary measure of intervening to cut that debate short and to prevent a vote from taking place on the concurrence motion.
This procedure of cutting short debate and preventing committees of this Parliament from reporting to the House of Commons and from having concurrence motions put and fully debated is an extraordinary measure and one which constitutes an attack upon the very basis of accountability in our system of government.
Any structure that any of us has seen which tries to lay out a blueprint for accountability in our government has as its core the Parliament of Canada, and any attempt made to disrupt the relationship between the committees of Parliament and the House of Commons itself is indeed an attack upon the proper functioning of this House of Commons.
I want to quote from a book which was published not that long ago by a former member of Parliament, John B. Stewart, who, after his defeat in the House of Commons, served as an adviser to the government on the question of parliamentary reform. He dealt with the procedure followed by the government in that instance, a procedure which is now being threatened by the government House leader. This is what he had to say about a procedure whereby at the end of the day, after a discussion had taken place, automatically a motion to concur would revert to government orders. I quote:
Since 1965 once a debate begun under Motions has been adjourned, the order for resumption of the debate is a government order. This means that the government House leader has the right to decide if and when the debate will be resumed. Clearly, this is an odious power. It gives the government the right to sidetrack a committee's report permanently.
Again, this was written by a former Liberal member of Parliament who served as an adviser to the present government. It was in his book entitled "The House of Commons: Procedure and Reform". If on a motion to concur it is odious that that motion should be transferred to government orders where the right and responsibility is then that of the government to decide whether it ever comes forward for debate again, how much more odious it is that the government would use its majority to intervene to prevent a debate taking place whereby, after the first speaker has spoken, moving that a report be concurred in, the government would intervene, use its majority and prevent other members of the committee from speaking, even its own members on the committee. This is what was done with the committee's fourth report in July. This

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments is what was threatened just last Thursday by the government House leader. It is a process which is indeed odious. It is an attack upon the very essence of ministerial accountability and responsible government of this country.
The government may say that Parliament has more impor-that business or that somehow it is not proper that Members of Parliament should ask that consideration be given to committee reports made to Parliament. This is the business of Parliament. There is nothing more fundamental. The business of Parliament is that individual members, particularly representatives of parliamentary committees, ensure that studies conducted on behalf of Parliament are brought to the attention of Parliament and that Parliament have the opportunity to debate them. Indeed, to deny this, to attempt to block that sort of progress from taking place, is to destroy the vital link that is so essential in our representative institutions in Canada today.
The government may say that the process has been abused in some way in the past. That is not so. It is interesting to note that in the past 12 years since 1969 when the government brought in its rules reforms which changed the whole functioning of Parliament, 160 concurrence motions have been moved of which 147 were carried. Of those, 133 were carried without debate and 115 of those were purely routine. Twelve were carried after debate. One of these was effectively a government motion. Six were debated part of the day and not carried. Five were debated a full day and not carried. An additional two were interrupted by government motion to end the debate. One of those two actions to interrupt the concurrence motion, and there were only two in the past 12 years, came in July when the government interceded to prevent discussion of that major report, the fourth report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
Of all those moved by backbenchers which took government House time, and there were 24, 15 were moved by opposition members. Since 1974, 14 motions required some debate and eight of those were from the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. In the session of 1980-81 a government backbencher moved a motion which carried after a short debate and a motion from the committee was interrupted by a government motion.
If you look at this history and the way this procedure is being used, it is clear that what the government threatened to do last Thursday and may do today is a break with the traditions of the House of Commons. It represents an important new attack upon the ability of committees to function. It is something which members of this Parliament should not be asked to agree with.
If it is essential that any committee be able to report to the House of Commons and be able to have discussion of its report, how much more essential is it when Parliament charges the standing joint committee to serve as a watchdog, to look at government regulations to determine whether they are legal in the first place, to determine whether due process or natural justice has been interfered with, to determine whether or not the issue being dealt with in a regulation should more properly be brought back before Parliament? When you have a watchdog committee such as this, how much more important is it in this case and in normal cases that the debate should take place and the committee should have the opportunity to have its report considered by the whole House of Commons?
What the government is doing when the government House leader comes before Parliament and says that the only basis on which he will not interrupt the debate and allow the committee to do its job is at the convenience of the government-when the government sees fit, if it sees fit, in its own time-is that it is taking that watchdog committee and trying to turn it into a lapdog committee.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He is asking that a watchdog committee check its teeth and put them in a glass by the bed. That is not acceptable in this day and age if we believe in parliamentary democracy and if we believe that we have a responsibility in this Parliament to supervise and scrutinize the activities of the government on behalf of Parliament.
In other jurisdictions there are procedures which provide in many instances that the government issue a white paper in responding to committee reports. In Australia it is mandatory that a white paper be issued within six months to respond to a committee report. A similar procedure is followed in Great Britain at the present time.
In some other jurisdictions there are provisions whereby, if individual members of Parliament have a concern about a regulation that is passed under delegated legislation, they have the ability to put down a motion of disallowance. For example, in the case of Australia, unless a debate is held, unless the House decides not to disallow a regulation within a certain period of time, the regulation will automatically be disallowed.
If we had that sort of procedure in the Canadian Parliament, perhaps it would be less important that we have some assurances that committee reports will be discussed. However, we do not have that. We recommended that in the report which was discussed in July. That has never been acted on by the government.
Let me quote from a book by Professor J. R. Mallory, "The Structure of Canadian Government", which deals with the essential nature of responsibilities of parliamentary committees and parliamentarians in keeping an eye on how the government acts with delegated legislation. I quote from page 140:
Parliamentary criticism is of the greatest importance. The chief defect of delegated legislation is precisely that it is passed without public debate and without serious opportunity for subsequent parliamentary review. Furthermore, regulations, unlike acts of Parliament, are not always published or collected in acceptable form so that the citizen can know what the law is that governs him. There is an old maxim that ignorance of the law is no excuse as a defence for breaking it. As long as the law is readily accessible to any competent lawyer who knows his way around the law reports and the statute books, this is a wise rule. But when the law consists of a multiplicity of detailed regulations which are not always easy to Find out about, the maxim becomes almost oppressive in its effect. Adequate parliamentary scrutiny and adequate publication of regulations have therefore become recognized as necessary accompaniments of the growth of delegated legislation in well-run communities.
October 26, 1981

That is a description by Professor Mallory, one of our most distinguished political scientists in this country, of the essential nature of activities that Parliament must undertake when scrutinizing actions by the government in delegated legislation. It is worth while looking back at the time in which the committee was created. At that time Tommy Douglas asked John Turner, the heir apparent, the "pretender to the throne" in Toronto, whether he felt it would be useful to have included in the statute a provision whereby reports of the committee could be acted upon and whether it would be compulsory. Mr. Turner responded by saying that he recognized it would be essential that the committee have the power to do its job, but the rules of the House of Commons already provided for that to be done and it was likely not necessary to have this written in the statute. Yet what we are finding today, Mr. Speaker, is that the promise made by Mr. Turner at the time the committee was established is being threatened with being broken because the government is threatening to intercede to prevent the committee from doing its job. That is why I call upon the government today, Mr. Speaker, to allow a full debate in this House on a matter that is of urgent concern to all Canadians.
I want to turn to the report itself, Mr. Speaker, which was tabled in the House of Commons on June 17, 1981. There were four points in the committee report which were considered essential and about which we felt it was important that we should make a report to the House of Commons and draw the attention of the House to the structure of VIA Rail and to some of the actions of the government.
First of all, in the setting up of VIA Rail we felt the government had acted in a way that did not provide for proper parliamentary discussion. We discovered VIA Rail was set up, using in part an Appropriation Act. Consequently, the House of Commons did not have a proper statute before it that would allow for a full and public debate on the part of Members of Parliament which would enable the government to put forward a comprehensive program for future railway passenger services in this country.
Obviously, that sort of provision would have been very valuable. Earlier this year when a question of privilege Was raised by one of my colleagues, Madam Speaker found that the procedure of acting through an Appropriation Act in a way that was attempting to get legislative action was wrong. She struck down a number of attempts by the government to do that. Indeed, had Madam Speaker been in the chair at the time this was done in 1977, the likelihood was that the government could not have brought VIA Rail Canada forward in this way. The likelihood would have been the government would have had responsibility, the necessity, of coming back before Parliament and the Canadian people and fully debating its plans for the future.
Let me briefly read to you, Mr. Speaker, the actual objection raised by the committee on this particular point. It said: VIA Rail Canada Inc. has been established and set up in business-and in consequence almost all of the railway passenger services of the country have been brought into government ownership, control and funding-pursuant to an
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
involved use of subordinate powers, a dollar vote in an Appropriation Act and the three slim regulations under report. At no time has Parliament had the opportunity to debate and to settle what are very significant matters.
I shall come back to this point shortly, Mr. Speaker, but let me now move on to the three substantive criticisms which the committee made in its report. The second criticism it made was this:
The operative dollar vote. Vote 52d, Department of Transport, Appropriation Act No. I, 1977, refers only to "selected rail passenger services", yet S.O.R./78-286, made under that vote, purports to apply not only to passenger services operated over railway lines but also to other passenger services, and not only those in substitution for rail services but also those ancillary to them.
What does this mean in plain English, Mr. Speaker? It means that when the government runs a bus service under VIA Rail or when it runs a limousine service, as it is doing in some parts of the country, and spends public funds to do so, it is acting in a way that has not been approved by Parliament. The expenditure of funds in that way may well be illegal.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be more important to this House of Commons than the question whether Parliament is given authority to spend funds in a particular way, or whether it is spending the money that belongs to the people of Canada improperly. At the present time there are a number of bus routes in this country which are run by the government; for example, Lindsay-Peterborough-Cobourg; Jasper to Banff; Prince Albert to Saskatoon; Edmonton to Calgary. And there are numerous others. The committee does not quarrel with the authority of the government to have buses. What we do quarrel with, even under the Appropriation Act which was initially used as an excuse for setting up VIA Rail, is that we can find no justification for the expenditure of public funds on those lines. Surely the government must come back to Parliament and seek Parliament's approval.
The third complaint raised by the committee was this:
An item critical to the funding of the services provided by VIA Rail Canada Inc., the ''prescribed portion" of the employee costs of the railway companies (for severance benefits, early retirement benefits and the like) in implementing the changeover to VIA Rail control of passenger services, has never been prescribed by a regulation under Vote 52d, but is contained in an unpublished, and hence unscrutinized, statutory instrument.
The government admitted there was an order in council that provided this particular authority. Under the procedures adopted by this government, that is considered an unscrutiniz-able order in council by the government. It is not published in The Canada Gazette and it is not considered by the government to be properly brought forward before the standing joint committee. Consequently, this action has not been proper and on the strength of what the government says is not properly before the committee for scrutiny. Clearly this is a practice, Mr. Speaker, that the committee has complained about in the past and that must be revised.
The report, fourthly, says this:
The prerequisites to or limitations on payment of the ''prescribed portion" need not be set out in a regulation. Any terms or condition subject to which payment is to be made that are set by the governor in council by regulation must be obeyed, but if the minister sets any others, they may, without their being embodied in any regulation, be embodied in the arrangements entered into with the railway companies. Thus, the very terms of what was a vital part of the VIA

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
Rail program were left to the minister to determine in conjuction with the railway companies.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that not only did we find the order in council was deficient because it was not published in The Canada Gazette, but further the order in council did not provide in many instances for these other actions. It is not included in the order in council. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, we felt it was important to bring this matter to the attention of Parliament.
Let me return to the question whether or not a VIA Rail Act is necessary. What need be done? One of the areas where there has been confusion is in government policy. All of the committee's report in appended to and printed in the Votes and Proceedings of Wednesday, June 17, 1981. It would be impossible for me to review all of the report in the short time I have available to me, but I want to recommend to all members of the House that they study the report and give consideration to the points raised therein. In particular, I also want to draw to the attention of the House Appendix "A", which includes a series of correspondence between the Minister of Transport and the committee.
This has been an issue that the committee has been dealing with for over two years, Mr. Speaker. The government says, "Be patient, don't call your motion for concurrence today, sooner or later we will get around to it." The committee perhaps has been too patient already. Over the course of two years we have been dealing with this particular issue, yet we have found letters have gone unanswered or we have had responses from the Minister of Transport which are confused and contradictory.
The first letter included in the appendix is June 26, 1980, when we wrote to the Minister of Transport to ask for an indication from him as to how the policy review which he referred to before about VIA Rail was proceeding. In particular it said:
The committee is anxious to know whether and when a bill for an act to provide for VIA Rail Inc. will be introduced.
That was on June 26. Almost two months later, on August 19, the Minister of Transport wrote back to the committee and said:
With respect to the possible introduction of a bill to provide for a VIA Rail Canada act, the cabinet submission which will seek decisions in respect of rail passenger services and of VIA Rail Canada Inc. is, in particular, now in the advanced stages of interdepartmental consultation.
This is over a year ago. He said further:
I anticipate that a cabinet decision on the issues raised in that submission will be available to use by the end of September.
September came and went, Mr. Speaker. On November 6, 1980, the committee wrote back again to the Minister of Transport and said:
We were instructed to ask whether the cabinet decision to which you referred has been taken and when you will respond to the committee's position on the need for the introduction of a VIA Rail Canada bill.
That was on November 6, Mr. Speaker. It took the minister until January 12 to respond to the committee's letter. His response at that time was:
"The cabinet has not yet considered the submission to which I referred in previous correspondence. I expect the matter to be discussed early in the new year. Once a decision has been reached, I will advise the committee on the requirements for a VIA Rail Canada bill.
We were then put off to the beginning of this year. On March 19, well after the beginning of the year had come and gone, Mr. Speaker, we wrote again to the Minister of Transport. We said this:
The committee wishes to have some definite time frame within which it can work and we are instructed to ask once again for some definite if not precise date by which a decision whether or not to proceed with a VIA Rail Canada bill will be taken. Mindful of the fact its position in this matter has been in suspense as it were since just before the March 1979 dissolution the committee has adopted a time limit of May 6, 1981 on the decision to place a special report before both Houses.
We wrote to the minister on March 19. We said that we wanted a response so that we could make a report to both Houses by May 6, which was a month and a half later. The letter from the minister was dated May 7, 1981, the day after the date we indicated in the letter to the minister that we wanted to report to the House. What was the minister's reply? He said:
At present, there does not appear to be an immediate requirement for a VIA Rail Canada act. Once the existing legislative framework has been sufficiently tested, it should be possible to establish whether a constituent act is definitely needed.
There is no existing legislative framework because there never was a VIA Rail Canada act. The minister said flatly at that point that he had made a decision that there did not appear to be any need for a VIA Rail Canada act and that he wanted to leave it off.
The committee indicated to him before that it wanted to report to the House the day before the minister sent his reply. We were patient again and waited for the minister. On May 21, 1981, we wrote again to the minister and said:
The committee is of the view that there is an immediate requirement for a VIA Rail Canada act and that the existing legislative framework, consisting of votes in Appropriation Acts which may not even support all the regulations already made, is inadequate. Your letter appeared to the committee to avoid answering the issue it has raised. Consequently, the committee feels that a report to the Houses is needed and will be considering this matter again on May 28 and June 4. In the meantime, we shall appreciate receiving immediate clarification of your statement that "a decision on the matter is not possible". Does this mean that the committee has been told nothing is now being done to bring in a VIA Rail Canada bill?
As instructed by the committee, we are sending a copy of this letter to the government House leader so that he will be on notice of the committee s opinion that speedy action should be taken to introduce VIA Rail Canada legislation.
That date came and went without a response from the minister. Finally the committee reported, and again the minister's response came in after the committee had reported to the House of Commons, after the time had elapsed.
What we see in this history is either incredible ineptitude on the part of the minister, that he is incapable, over the course of several months in some instances, of getting his department to prepare letters for him, or we find that the minister is deliberately and consciously attempting to insult a committee of both


October 26, 1981

Houses, withhold information from it, and make it impossible to continue its proceedings.
Following the presentation of the report and following the minister's response, we wrote him again in mid-summer. We have yet to receive a response to that letter. In checking with the minister's officials today we find that a response was drafted for him some months later again, on October 14, but the minister refused to sign the response and it has been sent back for redrafting. How can Canadians expect that the minister will run the transportation system in the country if he cannot run his own office, if he cannot answer his mail? Surely Parliament deserves better from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) than it has received to date.
A further complication was added earlier this year when, in response to a question by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), a former minister of transport, the minister responded in part to the committee's report. He indicated that as far as he was concerned he had made a conversion, he was now in favour of a VIA Rail Canada act. The House will remember that in the letter he sent to the committee, the letter upon which we acted, he indicated that he did not see any particular need, that he was quite happy to have this drag on, that it did not appear to be necessary. However, when the hon. member for Vegreville raised this matter in the House of Commons, it was made clear by the minister at that time that he had had a change of heart, that in fact he had decided that it would be useful to have such legislation. As reported on page 11454 of Hansard for July 13, 1981, the minister said:
Madam Speaker, on the first subject, I am not in a position to comment because the decision of cabinet has not been made. On the other subject, that is the usefulness, necessity of having a VIA act, I am in full agreement with the views expressed by the hon. member and others.
The problem has always been with the agenda or the timetable of the House. In 1977 when VIA was created by an item in the estimates, presumably there were too many items on the agenda of the House. Last year I gave priority to the problem of the transportation of dangerous goods. This coming year, as the hon. member knows, we have the ports policy to bring up. We also have the independent air safety board to create. Thus, time is really the problem. Everyone agrees that VIA is entitled to legislation of its own as one of the major Crown corporations. I am committed to cabinet to bring forward a memorandum on the subject which might lead to that realization, whenever the time of the House permits.
Again a reversal on the part of the minister. Initially when we wrote to him it appeared that he was sympathetic. That was over a year ago. Initially he appeared sympathetic, then he reversed himself, and in his letter in May he indicated that he was no longer sympathetic, that there was no need. Yet in July there was another reversal; there was a need but nothing would be done because he was too busy and Parliament was too busy. Nothing would be done to consider the report of the standing committee, to consider whether or not VIA Rail had been properly constituted, to consider whether the Parliament of Canada should have the opportunity to debate the government's comprehensive railway passenger program for the 1980s. Surely the minister insults hon. members of the House of Commons by saying that that matter is too trivial to be brought forward at this time. Surely we are entitled to have that act.
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
What does VIA feel about its position in this picture? I refer hon. members of the House to the 1979 annual report of VIA Rail Canada. In a report to shareholders, Mr. J. Frank Roberts, Chairman and President, said on page 5:
1979 clearly showed that the legislative and institutional framework within which VIA operates is inhibiting the corporation's ability to realize its full potential.
VIA's mandate is to provide Canadians with attractive, convenient passenger train services while reducing the cost to government. This is being interpreted as "serve the public regardless of the cost" at one end of the spectrum, while at the other, it is taken to mean "reduce expenses regardless of the consequences".
We know on which end of the spectrum is the minister. He continued:
It becomes therefore imperative that VIA's mandate and objectives be expressed clearly.
That is where the Chairman and President of VIA Rail Canada, speaking on behalf of VIA Rail, stands on this issue. Yet nothing has been done.
What did the Chairman and President say in the 1980 annual report? On page 4 of the 1980 annual report he said:
VIA has further defined its mandate as a rail passenger corporation, but until a clear mandate is approved by government, progress will be difficult.
If the government had acted properly in the first place, if it had brought forward a VIA Rail Canada act, if it had allowed debate to take place in Parliament, if it had disclosed its plans to the people of Canada, if there had been proper discussion here and throughout the country, we would not be in the situation we are in today-with confusion reigning, with the minister acting under an extraordinary procedure to cancel VIA Rail lines, with VIA Rail itself complaining that it simply does not know its own mandate. If this had been done properly from the outset, we would be concentrating on providing a fast, efficient and economical rail passenger service to Canadians. But because it was not, we find a serious deterioration in service, we find cancellations taking place in this manner, we find serious disenchantment both within VIA and the country at large.
What justification can there be after all these years for doing the proper thing which the minister in his most recent flip-flop acknowledged is necessary and should be done? Was Parliament's concern in this issue something which was discovered only of late? The answer is no. This was debated in Parliament. There were points of order when the government attempted to act this way in 1977. The committee made two general reports on regulations; one in the second session of the Thirtieth Parliament, 1976-77 and one in this session. Both of those dealt with what we feel is a faulty procedure followed by the government in using Appropriation Acts to confer legislative authority upon itself.
Since we made our report on VIA Rail, Madam Speaker, in response to a point of order which was raised on this side of the House, ruled that in fact the committee's concerns were justified and that in fact the concerns expressed at the time VIA Rail was created were justified. So this is not something new, Mr. Speaker; it is not a trivial and inconsequential

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments problem but one that goes to the heart and functioning of the rail passenger system in this country.
What will happen if the government continues to act in this way, Mr. Speaker? What will happen if it does not put a comprehensive program before Parliament? The first thing we will find is that the government will resort to the extraordinary measures it used to cancel 19 per cent of its rail passenger service. That is of concern to this House and to all Canadians today. Witnesses will appear before the committee tomorrow evening to discuss the propriety and the legality of the government's action and the Minister of Transport will appear before the committee on Thursday afternoon. We will welcome him at that time and give him an opportunity to explain why he has acted as he has.
As chairman of the committee, I do not want to prejudge the discussions that will take place. Suffice it to say that there is consternation in the country about the actions by the government; suffice it to say that there is sufficient concern that members of the committee felt it necessary that this matter should be investigated. I am sorry that the Minister of Transport has left the House and I recognize that he has other important business to attend to, but I put him on notice at this time that counsel for the committee has found serious doubts about whether the order cancelling those railways passenger services is valid. It may very well be null and void and that even using this extraordinary method the government bungled its attempt to achieve its ends. I put the minister on notice of that today. I hope that other government representatives in the House will ensure that he looks into the committee's concerns in this respect.
The committee is on record as believing in freedom of information and I would indicate to the minister as well, therefore, that the legal opinions offered to the committee are available to him and to the people of Canada.
If the government does not bring forward comprehensive legislation, then it will continue to use these extraordinary methods to create a piecework rail transport system without any over-all direction or without there ever having been a proper debate on the subject.
The next thing that will happen will be a retrenchment of railway passenger services. Through attrition the service will shrink, serving fewer Canadians, but it will continue to be paid for by the people of Canada, it will continue to suffer from very serious morale problems and it will continue to be the cause of vexation to Parliament. But most important, unless the government makes a commitment to rail passenger service for the future and spells out its plans to Parliament, VIA Rail will continue to die the death of a thousand cuts as line after line after line is abandoned and service after service withdrawn. I know that no member of the House wants to see that happen. All members want a fast, efficient, economical railway passenger service in this country. If we are to have that, it is essential that the government act now and does not allow the drift to continue.
I call on the government to allow members on all sides of the House, and in particular members of the committee, to debate
this report. I call upon the government today to put on record its intention to act without further delay on the committee's concerns and to confirm that it will allow Parliament to debate a full and comprehensive VIA Rail Canada act.
I will sit down before my time has elapsed, Mr. Speaker, but I want to establish that the onus is now on the government. The power is in the government either to act in the extraordinary way in which it acted last July by cutting short debate and preventing a parliamentary committee from doing its job, or by respecting the rights of Members of Parliament and the responsibility of a parliamentary committee and allowing a full debate in this House before any further action is taken.
I call upon the government today to do the right thing. I call upon it to allow the debate to take place. I call upon it to act without further delay on the report of the committee and to bring forward a comprehensive VIA Rail Canada act which will enable the country to have a rail passenger service second to none.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support strongly the motion for concurrence moved by the co-chairman of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. I must say that it is with a certain amount of surprise that I rise at this time. I am pleased to see that the government has not adopted the rather shoddy tactics it adopted on July 14 last when a similar motion was presented by the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty). Following his excellent presentation on behalf of a unanimous committee, the then parliamentary secretary to the President of the Privy Council stifled debate by moving a motion that the House proceed to orders of the day.
One can only speculate on why a similar motion has not been moved at this point. I would not want to suggest, of couse, that the reason such a motion was not put forward at this time is that the government might lose the vote; perhaps there are not enough government members in the House to carry the motion. I know that this is not necessarily accurate, or at least it is possibly not accurate.
I am pleased to be able to take part in the debate on this motion for concurrence in the revised seventh report of the committee. Before getting into the substance of that report, I should like to say that this committee does not operate in the limelight; it is a hard-working committee which virtually always operates on the basis of consensus. The only power of the committee, if it believes that the government has taken action which violates the criteria established for the committee, is to report to this House. On a number of occasions the committee has reported on matters of substance and matters of procedure. The last time a motion for concurrence in the committee's report was put forward was on the fourth report. That was not just a two or three-page report on a particular regulation or statutory instrument but was a report on the means by which the committee had been functioning, the role of the committee in making very serious recommendations for changes in the way in which regulations are promulgated and
October 26, 1981

reviewed, and the opportunities that the public has for input into the process of making regulations.
That report was treated with contempt; it has disappeared from the Order Paper so that, effectively, the government has rejected the recommendations of the committee without any meaningful debate.
I emphasize that it was the unanimous recommendation of the committee-Liberal and Conservative members from both Houses agreed and, also a member of the New Democratic Party-that there should be sweeping changes in the process of reviewing all regulations in this country. The government's response was to kill the report.
Today there is before the House a motion for concurrence in the seventh report of that committee. I hope that the government will see fit to accept its recommendations in a spirit of good faith, following debate. The government may contemptuously reject all recommendations for change that the committee put forward but I hope it will recognize the work done by the committee and support the motion for concurrence in the revised seventh report.
My colleague, the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe, has gone through the substantive elements of the report and the fact that members are deeply concerned about the way in which VIA Rail Canada was established by means of a procedural device known as a $1 vote. The effect of that procedure was to deny Members of Parliament, either in this chamber or in committee, any opportunity to debate the wisdom of creating this important corporation. That sets a very dangerous precedent for the future.
We are also concerned about the precedent which has been created by the establishment of this multimillion dollar corporation for future operations of the government. How many other procedural wrangles and devious devices of this nature will the government use in an attempt to bypass Parliament? We have already seen the way in which the government has chosen to ignore the views of literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians by bypassing the Canadian Transport Commission in chopping very fundamental and badly needed rail service throughout this country. Therefore, to suggest that the government may be establishing a precedent here, I would submit, is not being alarmist, but, rather, is a recognition of the trend which seems to be very much in vogue with this particular government.
It was not so very long ago that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that Members of Parliament, when they left this chamber, were nobodies. There seems to be a new philosophy with this government. Members of Parliament, not only outside the chamber but also inside the chamber, as far as this government is concerned are nobodies. It is that concern which was addressed by our fourth report, the report which the government killed and which has disappeared from the Order Paper. It is that concern to which the committee addressed itself in our seventh report, which is now before the House. As 1 stated, the establishment of VIA Rail by a $1 vote subverted
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
any opportunity of Parliament to debate the wisdom of the creation of this important institution which is being destroyed or, at least, seriously harmed by the actions of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
What was the response of the government to the concern which was expressed by our committee? Our concern was that at the very least a bill should be brought before Parliament creating VIA Rail Canada, in order that Members of Parliament on all sides of the House might have an opportunity to consider the wisdom of that. The response has been "yes" and "no", and "yes" and "no". I understand that the latest answer from the minister was "yes", in response to a question by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). As recently as May of this year, quoting from Appendix "A" to our report, we were told by the minister:
At present there does not appear to be an immediate requirement for a VIA Rail Canada act. Once the existing legislative framework has been sufficiently tested, it should be possible to establish whether a constituent act is definitely needed.
Of course, what this is saying is that the government, having established our committee, having accepted that this is an important committee, can pick and choose; and when we submit a report with which the government agrees, then it can graciously concur. However, when we submit a report which is in any way critical of the government, which it does not like, it can do one of two things: it can use its procedural gimmickry to kill the report, as it did with our fourth report; or it can permit a debate for a period of time, and then use its numbers to vote against the motion of concurrence.
I cannot believe that the Liberal members on this occasion would actually take that opportunity to vote against a motion of concurrence which is so vitally important to the nation and which so fundamentally affects not only VIA Rail, but also the way in which this Parliament works. Because that is the essence of this report. Indeed, the substance is important, the question of whether or not the minister can bypass Parliament, bypass elected representatives, and create this corporation. However, far more important is the way in which similar recommendations are treated by this government.
We are talking, indeed, about the role of this committee. As one member of that committee, I question the usefulness and validity of spending thousands of dollars of taxpayers' money-our counsel recently estimated something in the order of $200,000-and valuable hours of parliamentarians' time from all sides of the House in carefully considering regulations and statutory instruments if, when we decide as a serious matter that we must report to the House that the government has apparently violated certain of our criteria, the government can just sweep that report under the carpet and ignore it. What is the point of the committee? That is our only power: the power to report to this House; the power to hope that in good faith our reports will be considered on their merits by all members of the House.
In closing, I urge that the House give very serious consideration to this important motion, not only in terms of the substance of the seventh report which is before us, which is the

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
manner in which VIA Rail was created, but, far more importantly, as an indication of genuine response to the important issues which have been raised by this committee. It would be an indication of its importance that when this committee reports we do take seriously our mandate, and that this House, or a majority on the other side, does not contemptuously choose to ignore any criticism but responds to it in a positive and constructive manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should express my appreciation to the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson). I think it is fair to assume that after the understanding was made there was a disposition on our side to yield the floor to him. But on the other hand, the hon. member appeared to want to hear my words of wisdom first and elected to follow me.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise in my place this afternoon to support the motion presented by my colleague of concurrence in the seventh report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments. I want
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
to pay tribute as well to the co-chairman and the membership of this important committee, who I understand have worked in a very non-partisan way to attempt to uphold some of the traditions and principles of the institution of Parliament. I think their report is an excellent one.
However, I am saddened that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has been so derelict in responding to it. Nonetheless, he did indicate to the House last Thursday, when I had an opportunity to debate a question in the adjournment debate, that he did have the first draft of a VIA Rail act. That is certainly some progress, Mr. Speaker, but it is something which should have been placed before this House some time ago.
At the time VIA Rail was created by a $1 vote in the estimates, we took exception to the circumvention of parliamentary authority. VIA Rail has since grown into a full-fledged Crown corporation, and as late as July 27 and since then it has been the subject of a major national debate.
It seems to me the failure of the government to move toward the formal ratification of VIA Rail through the Parliament of Canada constitutes a very dismal failure on its part. The action to reduce, if not emasculate, Canada's rail passenger service which is operated by VIA Rail is indeed a shameful act which is causing deep anger, outrage and regional discord. It is creating very severe and grave implications for hundreds of thousands of Canadians who use and rely on rail passenger service. It will have some very serious consequences on the 1,600 people directly affected by these cutbacks, plus the hundreds of thousands of others who will be indirectly affected.
What is fundamental is that this government has failed to call upon Parliament to share in the formulation of rail passenger services in Canada as a major national policy. It seems to me that it is not asking too much to call upon the Parliament of Canada, its elected representatives and the people of Canada, those who are directly and indirectly affected by rail passenger services in this country, to come forth and contribute in the formulation of an over-all rail passenger policy.
The fact that VIA Rail was established by the stroke of a pen through a $1 item has disallowed that opportunity to Canadians. It has prevented the Parliament of Canada from establishing a mandate with goals and objectives which would govern the operation of VIA Rail. It does not have the necessary bargaining power at the present time because it lacks the kind of autonomy it should have as an ongoing business concern.
The reason for this is its outdated and archaic costing order. Under the basis of the present terms of reference and mandate, it is not able to deal with that in a realistic way. VIA Rail has failed to address the real needs of rail passenger services in this country because it has to go cap in hand to the government. It is the victim of the railways which constitute 63 per cent or more of VIA Rail's expenditures, an exorbitant cost, and that

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
leaves it very little room for manoeuvring. This 63 per cent expenditure is made without any control.
The R-6313 costing order is part and parcel of the failure of VIA Rail to function effectively and adequately in the discharge of rail passenger services along with its lack of a clear-cut parliamentary mandate outlining its goals and objectives and over-all global rail passenger policy for Canada. Those are the failings of VIA Rail today.
We have a situation now where a minister of the Crown can unilaterally and arbitrarily choose to reduce capriciously rail passenger services in this country by 20 per cent, inflicting very severe damage upon countless hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
I am not objecting to the principle of VIA Rail. As a matter of fact, during the course of our public hearings throughout Canada there was widespread support for the concept of VIA Rail. But the people that support VIA Rail would like to see a clearly defined mandate outlining VIA's goals and objectives. These Canadians would like to see it function as a bona fide Crown corporation which would have the mandate to deal on the basis of sound business principles.
I support the concept of VIA Rail but object to the fact that it was created in a haphazard manner. Canadians across this country are now paying for that carelessness. VIA Rail is now subject to the whims of a minister and government which, with the stroke of a pen, can reduce the service by 20 per cent.
What might we expect next year? The government may decide in its wisdom that the hon. Minister of Transport will have to reduce his budget further. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and the chairman of the economic development committee, who has over-all charge, may tell the Minister of Transport to shave another $100 million off his budget. Naturally, he will pick VIA Rail because its subsidies and expenditures are clearly defined. There is no difficulty in ascertaining what the government pays toward support of rail passenger services in this country.
It is not as easy to determine such a figure with respect to air transportation, surface transportation or even marine transportation.
If the Minister of Transport and this government is allowed to proceed with this drastic kind of emasculation of a service which is needed, it establishes a very dangerous precedent.
I point out again, next year it could cut back another 20 per cent or unilaterally abandon more branch lines. The basic branch line network in western Canada is not very safe if this is allowed to continue. The minister might even suggest as a cost cutting measure a cutback in ferry services support. These issues have to be dealt with.
When the archaic R-6313 costing order is coupled with the lack of an appropriately defined VIA Rail mandate, one arrives at the central core of what constitutes the failure of VIA Rail. Those two items must be dealt with.
We must have a clearly defined VIA Rail act. We must have an upgraded and realistic costing order, similar to what
Amtrak has in the United States whose cost of services provided by the railroad amount to 25 per cent of the budget. VIA Rail pays more than 63 per cent, close to two thirds of its total budget, on services that are provided by the railroads. One clearly gets the picture when one looks at the sleazy and slippery way in which these cutbacks were put into effect and the failure of the government to address costing order R-6313.
The government has shied away and continues to shy away from public debate. I cannot figure out why it refuses to hold public hearings. If the minister and his colleagues embarked on public hearings as our party chose to do during the summer, they would have been able to gauge the depth of the feeling there is for maintaining an effective and adequate rail passenger service in this country.
Maritimers especially are outraged by the fact they are going to lose their rail passenger service. They are not going to have alternative forms of service. I am sure the minister does not realize that maritimers rely more heavily on rail passenger service than does any other region of Canada. Time after time we heard witnesses testify that the railroad was part of the deal with confederation and they would not have been a member of confederation if they had not been promised adequate and effective rail passenger service.
