speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, they went so far as to say "Constitution be damned. Rail passenger service, yes. That is what we need." Maritimers are losing their rail passenger service and do not have an opportunity to express their views or challenge the minister.
Suspicions? There certainly are suspicions with respect to the accuracy of the figures and statistics that were given as background to the formulation of this decision. Time and again we heard the charge that revenues have been understated and expenditures overstated. We have heard people say time and again what would happen if their rail passenger service was taken away. One lady said it would be tantamount to cutting the heart out of New Brunswick.
It is the taxpayers of Canada who are paying to support VIA Rail service. Why can we not give the taxpayers of Canada the opportunity to share in the formulation of an effective rail passenger policy? We could do it under a VIA Rail act. We could have a beneficial debate in the House of Commons as well as across the country which would establish the needs in every region. We could educate Canadians to what it really costs to provide service, and then they could make up their minds whether they believe we should have a luxury type of service, a standard type of service, intercity services, regional or local services or transcontinental services.
The fact is that since the announcement of the minister this kind of assessment has been taking place. There are no less than four alternatives which are now on the table which could be used in exchange for the decision the minister has advanced. Transport 2000 has advanced an alternative pro-
October 26, 1981

posal. The government of Alberta has advanced an alternative proposal. VIA Rail itself has come out with an alternative proposal on re-equipping the transcontinentals, which would provide better service, reduce costs and put rail passenger service into the current technological era.
Indeed, there are rumblings from the minister's own department that there are better ways of achieving his objectives than the one he chose. There are rumblings from his department which take issue with the way in which the minister chose, unilaterally and arbitrarily, to reduce rail passenger services in this country.
The infamous leaked document which got into the hands of the Toronto Star said this, and I quote:
Only July 27 ... the government announced widespread changes in VIA Rail ... These changes have been approved by the governor in council, by means of an order in council varying Canadian Transport Commission orders and directives, and are to be implemented on November 15, 1981.
We have seriously questioned the propriety of a minister's invoking Section 64 of the National Transportation Act on a decision taken by the CTC more than two or three years ago. I find that really incredible because I do not believe Section 64 was ever intended to be used as a policy-making device. It seems to me that Section 64 was to give the governor in council an opportunity to deal with a timely and recent decision rendered by the CTC. If this government did not like the decision of the CTC back in 1977 or 1978, it should have invoked Section 64 at that time. It should have rescinded, amended or changed that decision in any way, shape or form it chose, but it refused to do that. It accepted that CTC decision and, two or three years later, it comes along and says, "Oh, but today we do not accept it, so we are going to amend it." That is wrong. That violates the spirit of the National Transportation Act, and it violates the intent for which Section 64 was to be used. Furthermore, it deprives the affected parties of the opportunity of natural justice.
As hon. members will recall, when considering whether to abandon or to expand rail passenger service or any mode of service in the country, the CTC used the criteria of public convenience and necessity to render its decision. It rendered a decision on the criteria of public convenience and necessity, and that is enshrined in the spirit of the National Transportation Act. Any movement away from that, in my view, is clearly challengeable. If the minister wants to change that fundamental part of the National Transportation Act, then he should bring in an amendment to the National Transportation Act, and we would debate it. However, the minister has not done that. He has chosen to hide behind the powers of Section 64, and I believe he is wrong. I believe he is violating the intent of Section 64 and the spirit of the National Transportation Act.
I am very happy that my good friend, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger), is in the House because I respect his views on transportation. I know he has worked with the CTC. I listened to him very carefully the other day when he said, with a great degree of clarity and assurance, that the minister was very much engaged in proper action consistent with the provisions of the National Transportation Act and Section 64 when
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments he arbitrarily chose to cut back rail passenger service by 20 per cent. Notwithstanding the alleged legality of it, it is morally wrong, and it breaks with the democratic and traditional way of doing things in this country. I hope the hon. member will welcome the challenge in the courts respecting Section 64 because I think-and the hon. member will agree with me- that if this action by the minister goes unchallenged, it will represent a very dangerous precedent which we in this chamber will live to regret.
The document leaked from within the Department of Transport goes on to say that to accomplish this decision-
-the government has used Section 64 of the National Transportation Act in an unprecedented manner.
That is what we are saying. I do not think it has ever been used in this fashion in the 50 years of the CTC and its predecessor, the Board of Transport Commissioners. That is why it is dangerous, and that is why it is wrong.
Instead of using the section as its drafters intended to vary the odd CTC order it did not agree with, the government is using it to restructure the whole VIA system.
The government is using Section 64 to restructure the whole VIA system. I get back to the thrust of the committee report, and that is the fact that VIA has been improperly constituted in a parliamentary sense. The matter should be brought before the House of Commons for full debate, and VIA should be fully mandated by the Parliament of Canada. So doing would give the members of this House and the people of Canada an opportunity to outline and formulate a clear-cut rail passenger policy for Canada. The government has failed to do that, and it continues to circumvent the issue and either break the law or come close to breaking the law. This government is very famous for that, and it is time it was challenged on every count.
The document goes on to state:
This is being done without CTC public hearings and without parliamentary scrutiny. Announcement of the changes was deliberately help up until Members of Parliament had left for the summer recess.
There you have it.
As best as can be determined, those responsible for the policy were so intent upon maintaining secrecy that only a limited number of government and VIA headquarters officials decided upon the detailed changes. The cabinet apparently then ordered further changes according to ministers' wishes, resulting in as uninformed and inconsistent an exercise in transportation planning as could be imagined. It appears that two particularly valuable sources of expertise, the CTC and VIA's own regional officers, were deliberately excluded.
It goes on to state:
It must be acknowledge that VIA's costs generally seem to be escalating rapidly and that several of the government's proposed cuts could be made without great hardship. The premise of the present alternative proposal is that roughly the same magnitude of saving could be realized by a proper and even-handed planning exercise, rather than the one conducted hurriedly behind closed doors by a small number of officials.
The document goes on further to outline an alternative proposal to the minister's decision which would result in an estimated $2.4 million per year saving in addition to the $100 million the minister alleges he will save. That is $2.4 million more than the government's proposal and, at the same time, "The Atlantic" would be salvaged and the western transconti-

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
nental would be salvaged. However, what we are looking at here is the kind of gimmickry and illegal tactics in which this government engages. It is absolutely shameful. It is the process as much as the decision that is causing anger and outrage throughout the country.
The government should allow a full-fledged public debate on VIA Rail. It should bring in legislation outlining its policy parameters, refer it to the standing committee and let the committee travel across the country to hear the views of the people. Is that asking too much? The transport committee has always been one of the most prestigious committees of the House of Commons. We have a railway committee room. This is because transportation is so important to this country.
If the government brought in a VIA Rail act, it would find there is widespread support for the concept of VIA, particularly at this time with high energy costs. VIA has not been given a fair chance to prove itself. More and more people are choosing to ride the trains, 41 per cent more today than when VIA took over. The government would find that rather than cutting back on rail passenger service, the people of Canada would recommend an expansion. There needs to be an upgrading of equipment.
Let us look at the Canadian Transport Commission decision of 1977-78. In addition to the establishment of the route structure some specific orders were made having to do with improvements in rolling stock, sleeping accommodation, meal service, scheduling and marketing. Those orders have not been fulfilled notwithstanding that ridership has increased by 41 per cent.
The government will not refer this decision to the Canadian Transport Commission or a standing committee because it is afraid of the truth, afraid to hear what the people have to say. The government did not talk about cutting back VIA rail service during the last election campaign. Now it is moving unilaterally and arbitrarily because it thinks the people will forget by the time the next election campaign rolls around. The people will not forget about this. I said the other day that instead of "twin-track Trudeau" we now have "No train Pepin". That is what it amounts to.
There is massive objection across Canada to the cutbacks in rail services proposed by the minister. There is massive outrage with regard to the arbitrary manner in which this decision was made. There is a very deep concern about the future of the Canadian Transport Commission. What is its role? It has suffered an end runaround in this case. It has been circumvented and emasculated. Who will be the protector of the public interest in terms of ensuring that we have adequate transportation service for all modes, air, surface and marine?
The people of Canada who appeared at the very extensive hearings in 1976 and 1977 believed that the decision was reached after all the evidence was presented to establish a rail passenger framework which was then described as being at an irreducible minimum. Any modification of that should automatically be referred back to the CTC. In its policy
directive to the CTC, the former minister of transport said among other things that the government wanted the CTC to establish a single spine transcontinental network. The CTC rejected that on the basis of public convenience and necessity. The commission found and ruled that under that criteria the service requirements could not be fulfilled with a single spine network. As I said earlier, if the government disapproved of that, it should have invoked Section 64 at that time. To do it now is wrong and in violation of the spirit of the act and the intent of Section 64.
If the government brought forth a VIA Rail act and deferred its decision to cut back, it would find through the voice of public opinion that the economic and social impact will be far more serious than it had considered. For that reason there has to be some check and balance. The government cannot unilaterally and arbitrarily, without any recourse to public input, do an end run on the people of Canada. It will find that the people of northern Ontario, particularly in those areas which will not have an alternate service, the lower income groups, the trappers, fishermen, outriggers and those in the Indian communities will be very seriously affected.
Many members on this side spoke about the impact on the tourist industry. If the government allowed the committee to go across the country, it would find that VIA Rail and rail passenger service is becoming a very major and integral part of tourist marketing in this country. The Japanese, Americans and Europeans who come here to visit the Rocky Mountains and the many attractive places in the Atlantic region use VIA Rail. There is a really blossoming tourist industry which centres around VIA Rail.
We heard during the hearings that people find it strange that on one hand the government pours hundreds of millions of dollars through DREE grants into the tourist industry in Atlantic Canada, and then another minister comes along and wipes out rail passenger service. How inconsistent and contradictory. The government would find as well that any reduction in rail service would have a very significant impact on our total tourist industry and therefore our balance of payments. It could see the discord and regional tension that would be created.
If the federal government brought forward a VIA Rail act and allowed the transport committee to go across the country to get the views of Canadians, it would find that the regions of the west and Atlantic Canada where the bulk of the cuts will take place would be most affected. Job loss will take place in those areas where there is the highest level of unemployment.
Any mention of the fact that moneys will be transferred from Atlantic Canada and western Canada to further support services in the Quebec-Windsor corridor will cause anger and tension. In that area there is now a multiple choice of transportation services.
It is interesting to note that in its submission to the transport standing committee, Voyageur Bus Lines very dramatically indicated that it was absolutely opposed to VIA Rail cutbacks, and the emphasis being diverted to the Quebec-Windsor corridor. Quite frankly, the traffic generated by
October 26, 1981

Voyageur along the Quebec-Windsor corridor is an important source of revenue for supporting other routes which are not so viable. Thus, that support is required to finance the not so heavily travelled runs.
What is going to happen by concentrating VIA Rail's efforts on the Quebec-Windsor corridor is that you may very well be putting a viable bus industry in jeopardy, certainly putting an industry in jeopardy to the extent that it is going to be forced to cut back on its less heavily travelled runs. This should be another matter considered in any over-all rail passenger policy.
There are many things that can be said about the present level of VIA Rail transportation. Suffice it to say it is not the time to be cutting back. It is not the time to be reducing rail passenger services, for a number of reasons. I have not mentioned the energy issue. Since we now have an oil agreement that is going to see fuel prices rise to $4 and $4.50 per gallon, surely it is incumbent upon us to take another look at all modes of public transportation, and surely it is incumbent upon the legislators of Canada to study the implications. This is new evidence which I believe has not been considered but should be considered. This also could be considered if we had a VIA Rail act brought before this House.
It has been said that VIA has suffered because it has been an illegitimate offspring and has suffered four and a half years of neglect. I believe this is an accurate reflection, because VIA was charged with the job of doing almost the impossible. The contractual arrangements and the costing arrangements that were put in place should be completely overhauled and reviewed. There should be no cutbacks based upon a costing order that is archaic and out of date. The CTC found it out of date. The CTC says that it has to be overhauled and has to be changed. The contractual arrangements have to be changed. VIA lacks the kind of autonomy it requires in order to do the job it is asked to do.
What about the historical and the statutory obligations of the railways? What responsibilities do they have in terms of maintaining rail passenger services? Under Sections 260, 261 and 262 of the Railway Act there are still some very clear statutory obligations for the purpose of maintaining adequate accommodation for passenger traffic and freight traffic. Those are items that should also be brought to the attention of the government and to any House committee that would be considering a new mandate for VIA Rail.
What about the question of energy efficiency? When we are looking at VIA Rail and the future of transportation in this country, surely it is time to come up with a clear analysis so that we may determine once and for all what is and is not the most energy-efficient mode of transportation. Surely it is time once and for all to establish what forms of public transportation are subsidized more than others, to what extent the highway mode is subsidized and to what extent the air mode, the marine mode and the rail mode are subsidized. We have various conflicting figures. Everyone uses their pet set of figures to argue their specific point.
Adjournment Motion
Clearly the time has come when all of these things must be put on the table and properly analysed and considered so that we can end up with the best kind of transportation system in this country. I am not simply pleading a case for rail passenger service. There is no question that we need all modes of transportation. But we must adopt intermodal concepts so that we can use the various modes in the most efficient and effective way possible. We will not do this unless we have an opportunity to debate a transportation policy and, particularly, a rail passenger policy. I believe this is the issue we are addressing ourselves to today in the substance of this particular motion.
I appreciate the opportunity to put some of my thoughts before the House, not only on the legality but some of the pitfalls, obstacles and difficulties that VIA Rail faces in terms of operating under its present structure. The fact of the matter is that VIA does not have an adequate structure to discharge the job it was asked to do.
If this motion is adopted and carried, it will compel the Minister of Transport to bring in a VIA Rail act which we can consider in depth, with the fullest of debate and in a manner where we would not be faced by a guillotine on November 15 which would emasculate and destroy the real heart and core of VIA Rail's route structure. Surely this is not asking for too much.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has talked at great length about the fact that we have waited some 50-odd years to get a Constitution. I am sure another year of deliberate consideration of this important subject that affects the hearts and minds and welfare of Canadians from coast to coast is in order. Why the haste? Why do we not just sit back and try to do something right? At a time when other countries are expanding rail passenger services, surely now is the time Canada should join that club. We can join that club by moving this motion forward. I hope members on the other side of the House will see fit to support it.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this debate on a question of procedure in the House. It is a question of how Members of Parliament are going to regulate their affairs and how the House is going to conduct its business in the most efficient way with a view to having the fullest hearing on the issues.
A report of the joint standing committee has been tabled in the House. Before we proceeded to orders of the day, a motion was made for concurrence of this report. The government, through the task forces it has launched, through the various committees and reports put before Parliament, has commenced a process of involving more parliamentarians to reach out further than the executive branch ever hoped it could to listen to Canadians, to talk to Canadians and to bring their views before this House. We must not cut this important, progressive move off at a very initial state, at a very tentative stage of its youth.
We are proposing a process whereby Members of Parliament, through joint committees that will involve hon. senators with their experience and wisdom, as well as members of all parties in the House, members who have expertise along with those who want to become experts in the subjects, go out and do their job.
I want to commend the standing joint committee, of which the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) is a member, for the work the committee did on its fourth report on the whole process of regulatory reform. I also commend the committee for the work it has done in its subsequent report. But I am not talking about the substance of the report that is before us today. I am talking about the process which could be used to stifle the authority of these task forces and committees in the future of our parliamentary system.
The hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) said that the government was stifling debate in wanting to get to orders of the day when we dealt with this matter previously. He said that the report had disappeared from the Order Paper and that, in effect, the government had rejected it. He asked; "What is the point of the committee?" The point of the committee was very important. The committee made its report. It was made public. It formed part of the legislative record which would act as a touchstone for legislation in the future. We have had a debate on VIA Rail in the House.
Let me turn to the specific proposals contained in the seventh report. It deals with the question that there was a $1 vote in 1977 which was the essence of our proceeding to cut VIA Rail. Let us look at this process. Nowhere in the record could I find any criticism of that measure which was taken and the possibility which was opened up in 1977. I challenge hon. members of the opposition to show us anywhere where that issue was challenged. The seventh report of the standing joint committee indicates nowhere that the procedures being adopted are illegal. Also the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) stated on a number of occasions that he intended at some future time to bring in a VIA Rail act. He has assured us that the government will be presenting this House with VIA Rail legislation for the future. As the minister explained so lucidly to the House, at the present time he is dealing with a crisis in cost.
I should like to return to the seventh report in which reference was made to the fourth report and the work of the previous committee of which the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe was a member. I must confess that he provided a great deal of leadership in terms of the fourth report which dealt with the entire process of regulatory reform. I only wish that his hon. colleague, Senator Godfrey, could be with us in the chamber today to assist in the debate of this particular issue. His learned contribution to the entire process of regulatory reform created another touchstone for Members of Parliament as we look to the future of our various committees and the roles each individual can play.
The seventh report reads in part as follows:
Your committee's predecessor called for an end to this practice inimical to parliamentary sovereignty. It should stop and all existing subordinate laws made under votes should be the subject of review as to merits by the appropriate parliamentary standing committee.
This is a clarion call for a new system and a new approach. I recall the words of the hon. House leader when the standing joint committee presented its fourth report. The hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe moved concurrence at that time, and the response of our House leader was that we had taken under consideration the very important proposals which have been put forward. He indicated that we agreed with many of them but that other reports had been put forward as well. There was the Lambert commission, the first report of the Economic Council and the report of the parliamentary task force on regulatory reform of which I was pleased to be chairman. This task force was very ably served by hon. mem-
October 26, 1981

bers from both sides of the House. Also there was the final report of the Economic Council of Canada which was published recently.
Within the last several years there have been a number of reports before the House dealing with the entire process of regulatory reform. The fact that the government created task forces and mandated various bodies to deal with the issue surely testifies to the good will on this side of the House to ensure the regulatory process goes ahead. I need only refer hon. members to the budget debate of last year in which the then minister of finance twice referred to the fact that regulatory reform was a priority of the government and that through proper regulatory reform we could indeed reduce the burden of regulation on the private sector in Canada and make regulators more accountable to Parliament and to the people of Canada.
This is why I am happy to rise on this particular issue. I felt somewhat taken aback when the hon. House leader of the official opposition quickly rose from his seat when he saw me rise to speak. I felt that he was suspicious. I do not know why he would want to be suspicious. Perhaps he felt that I was rising to try to stifle debate on this particular issue. I assure him that I was prepared at that time to defer to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) for whom I have a high regard. He has fought for particular issues with great eloquence in the House. We on this side of the House are pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this matter.
In connection with the entire process of regulatory reform about which we are talking, I should like to indicate that we are talking about the process by which regulations and rules are made and about the process of subordinate legislation. I bring to the attention of the House-and this is the first opportunity we have had to do it-a number of proposals put forward in our report which were concurred in by the fourth report of the standing joint committee. There has been widespread feeling that the exercise of ministerial discretion should be subjected to greater control. Perhaps this view is best expressed by Dicey. I should like to quote from the "Law of the Constitution" in which this learned jurist said:
The rule of law is contrasted with every system of government based on the exercise by persons in authority of wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers of constraint.. , Whenever there is discretion there is room for arbitrariness... Discretionary authority must mean insecurity for legal freedom on the part of its subjects.
This statement was made by the honourable jurist in 1885. Since that time I believe his words have held true, but the circumstances in our country and throughout the entire free world have changed dramatically. Government is much more a fact of life than it was then. Laws to protect consumers and individuals, to protect and help small businesses, to control abuses in many aspects of our lives, have become much more paramount. We in the task force found that many departments had amendments to regulations which they wanted to bring forward. They required amendments which had to be brought before the House. Some of them had been trying for four or five years to have their amendments put on the Order Paper. But we know that the House is blocked. There are so many
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments bills on the Order Paper which deserve the urgent attention of hon. members that we know we cannot operate strictly through the House. Therefore we have developed a system of delegating legislation to ministers to operate in certain areas. The standing joint committee has a watchdog role over the exercise of discretion. Let none of us confuse the fact that while we believe in the rule of law, the government could not effectively carry out its roles and responsibilities without having recourse to subordinate legislation.
Let us consider the admonition of Mr. Justice Brandeis who put the need for control this way: "Power must always feel the check of power". Also we should consider the words of Sir Richard Cartwright, the great grandfather of Chief Justice Cartwright, who said in 1912:
No man and no party can be safely entrusted with uncontrolled power.
The question before the House is not a question of the abuse of uncontrolled power. We have had members speak on this particular issue of VIA Rail and many members spoke in various ways. Some members on this side of the House have condemned certain of these closings, as have hon. members opposite.
Members have talked in the past about the need to control unnecessary expenditure. Members who have appeared before the transportation committee will realize that in many cases buses and alternate modes of transportation could serve us better than rail, so let us approach the question of transportation with an open mind.
The whole question of the process of regulatory reform is not the same here as in the United States. Hon. members opposite are getting quite excited about the process of regulatory reform. I would have thought they would be among the vanguard of those who seek to improve the accountability of the executive branch of the legislative arm. I welcome the attention of hon. members opposite given to what this House is trying to do.
I want to speak at some length about efforts that are being made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) to bring about regulatory control and reform. Before I go to that, however, I think it is important to mention that the process of regulatory reform in Canada is not one of so-called "deregulation"-getting the government off our backs, as we have seen take place in the United States. We have not looked upon this as a new political clout or a new way of dealing with things. What we are looking for is the creation of better regulation. We do not want to prejudge whether all regulation is good or bad; we want a better process forjudging regulation.
My thesis today is that we have many ways of controlling regulation, the exercise of ministerial discretion, but that none of these controls of themselves is entirely adequate or appropriate to the present day realities in this House. I should like to examine some of the controls that are exercised over the exercise of ministerial discretion, and draw to the attention of members of the House a statement made by Mr. Justice Rand who, I believe, was Canada's foremost civil libertarian and its

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
greatest constitutional expert. In the famous case Roncarelli v. Duplessis, the late Mr. Justice Rand said that "there is no such thing as absolute and untrammelled discretion".
Our courts have a history of attempting to wrestle with the question of when they have a right to intervene and upset the exercise of discretion by a minister acting in his executive capacity. In a number of cases it is held that orders in council are not in the category of legislative action; that they are not in the area of an exercise of rule-making that broaches on the border of being judicial. When that exercise of discretion does not have a judicial character to it, basically the courts have held that that exercise was an administrative action or a legislative action and could not be reviewed by the courts.
In this country we have a hodge-podge of cases on this subject. Suffice it to say that the jurisprudence which has arisen has admitted of no easy answers. It is very difficult to determine when a court can intervene to exercise control over the exercise of ministerial discretion.
There are four conclusions that follow from these cases. First of all, there is no law which says that minimal procedural standards, such as the right to notice of a hearing and a hearing itself, are conditions precedent to the exercise of ministerial discretion.
Second, the cases indicate that it is very difficult to decide when a judicial review is or is not open to an individual who feels aggrieved by the exercise of that discretion.
Third, I do not believe that to take every case before a court is a proper solution; rather, I believe that we have to find ways to amend our procedures for dealing with the exercise of discretion so that as legislators we can exercise the type of control that we have a responsibility to our constituents to exercise.
This type of review of our executive decision-making of regulations is going to become even more important with the introduction in the not too distant future, I hope, of a bill of rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That charter will make all subordinate legislation subject to its terms and conditions to ensure that there are no discriminatory laws or regulations which impinge unfairly on Canadians.
What are the types of controls that are exercised, apart from judicial review which, as I have indicated, is not in my opinion an adequate, although proper, type of exercise of control over the exercise of ministerial discretion? There are others.
There is the work of the standing joint committee which reviews the legality of regulations. The only problem is that the committee cannot review the merits of regulations. 1 believe it is proper that members of the House should have an opportunity to review the merits of regulations before they become law or after they have become law, with a view to being able to comment on whether they are good for Canadians or bad for Canadians-whether they are cost effective or are the most effective regulations we could have.
Another way that our regulators are influenced-and all Members of Parliament are subject to this-is by lobbying. Each of us is subject to lobbying. I use that word not in the
pejorative sense that it has acquired in many jurisdictions but in the most complete sense of lobbying, such as when a constituent comes to his or her member with a problem and says that the law should be changed. I think that is lobbying. We all know that lobbying is done on an extensive scale in Canada. People who represent institutions such as consumers' groups, farm groups, or business groups established in Ottawa, tell us that they want changes made to particular laws. I am concerned about some of the input that we receive. If we as regulators and lawmakers want to do our job effectively, then we need as much input as possible; but that input should come before we legislate and regulate.
There are some in our society who are not equipped to make their views know to us, in my opinion. It is very difficult for an individual to appear before a board that sets rates for telephones, for rail transportation or air passage. Very few consumers have the wherewithal to enable them to appear before government officials to try to convince them that prices should not increase in various areas. I therefore feel that we have to bring back together the collective public interest groups; those who do not have the funds to establish an office and a paid lobbyist in Ottawa to deal with us.
I believe we have on obligation to help bring together those collective grievances of small individuals who cannot otherwise deal with the issues. This would help us as legislators, on all sides of the House, more effectively to do our job as their wishes, views and alternatives would be known to us. This is why our task force on regulatory reform made a very strong and urgent plea that we introduce laws which will help, aid and abet public interest groups in their funding. The Consumers Association of Canada does an admirable job of appearing before many boards and committees; its biggest problem is not in deciding which hearings to attend, but in deciding how many hundreds every year it cannot attend because it does not have the funds at its disposal. There are similar examples of public interest groups.
Within the spirit of this motion before us dealing with the process by which regulations are enacted, I would therefore ask that hon. members from all sides of this House give greater consideration to the possibility of extended funding for public interest groups so that they can make their views known and legislators can have a balanced input to better do their job.
Another part of this process of having better, more effective regulations, of course, is access to information. We as individuals in this House know the importance of having access to information and full and complete information before we debate and decide upon an issue. This is why I urge the co-operation of hon. members opposite as the access to information bill proceeds through committee, so that we can get it before the House and get it passed. I believe it will have a significant impact in informing Canadians and helping us to inform ourselves.

speechtext:
We will not abuse it. We would hope that hon. members from the opposition would not use this process as an abuse in the future.
The major point that was made by the task force on regulatory reform was reiterated by the Economic Council, and was again reiterated by the standing joint committee in its report on regulations. I think the major issue was that governments must consult. Legislators must consult with their constituents and with effective public groups before regulations are passed. We believe that the private sector has a great role in helping us, as legislators, pass more cost-effective, responsive regulations. That type of consultation must go on, we believe, before channel vision takes place among our public servants.
The private sector, with the exception of public interest groups, has the facilities, the funds, the resources and the knowledge to enter into a collaborative effort with government to assist government in proposing and enacting better regula-
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments tions. This is why we must ask ourselves, in conjunction with the private sector with which we must consult: What are the problems we are seeking to resolve? Is government intervention really necessary to resolve them? Are there alternative types of intervention which might offer better solutions? Will the costs of regulation and the costs of setting up a control mechanism outweigh the benefits that we hope to derive from it?
When we intervene with regulations, we must always ask ourselves: Who will be the winners and who will be the losers? We know that when we impose any type of burdensome regulation on one sector of society, be it business, consumers or whatever, another side will have to pay for it. To me, this is the clarion message which springs from the final report of the Economic Council. It looked at regulations in the transportation industry, and that is what we should be looking at. It looked at regulations in the agricultural industry and in a number of other industries, and it attempted to assess the costs. What were the costs of those regulations? Who was paying for them? In many cases, the council said that it was the consumer of Canada who was paying for regulation in those areas. I think that the report of the Economic Council of Canada will serve us well in the future, because we will hesitate to regulate until we have assessed the costs in advance.
When we attempt to impose controls on one group or another, we will ask: Who is the winner? Who is the loser? Are consumers really benefiting? Are individual Canadians really benefiting, or is it only one industry or one small segment? When we have answered those questions, we will then be able to regulate with much more clarity and precision.
I had the pleasure of yielding to the hon. member for Vegreville. I always benefit from listening to his views, although I do not always agree with his views. He mentioned a very important point. He said that it was never intended that Section 64 of the National Transportation Act should deal with the situation in which we find ourselves concerning VIA Rail.
As Your Honour is aware, Section 64 deals with the right of appeal from a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission to cabinet. The reason for the creation of the Transport Commission and the many boards and agencies that we have in so many areas was to take advantage of the collective expertise and wisdom which exists in a commision through which it can undertake a consultative process in measures and make those available to us. However, I profoundly believe that because a board has made a decision we, as the executive, legislative branch, are not relieved of political responsibility for that decision. That decision affects Canadians, and it is one to which I, as Member of Parliament for Willowdale, am held accountable to my electorate.
Therefore, I would not want to take away the power of cabinet, under Section 64 of the National Transportation Act to step in where it disagrees with a decision of a board or commission and to say, "You have considered this, but we have an alternative view." In the past we have done this. For example, I refer Your Honour to a case where a cabinet

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments overruled a decision of the CRTC on a Bell rate increase. We felt, in our political judgment, that the rate was excessive; therefore, we rolled it back.

1 excuse myself from that remark, of course. I am merely a very proud member of the Liberal party and a member of this side of the House. What we did was step in and exercise our responsibility.
We do not want to strip the CTC of this right to have its decision appealed to cabinet. Our executive branch is prepared to assume that responsibility and be held accountable by the people of Canada. I do not hear any members on that side of the House condemning either of those two decisions about which we were speaking. We want to keep that power, and whether there are differences among members of this House, let us not in our haste, because of a particular issue, do away with a principle that has served us well in the past and has served Canadians well.
As part of this process of having a good interrelationship between the legislative branch and boards and tribunals, which we created to help us with their expertise in specialized areas, we also need a concomitant right of the cabinet to provide input and political direction on a timely basis, as the hon. member has said, so that cabinet directives can go out indicating government direction and government policy to these boards and agencies. That is not political interference. Boards and agencies will welcome that type of political direction. In the extensive hearings before our committee we were told they wanted that type of input.
One of the major issues that we addressed, apart from prior consultation about the necessity of funding public interest groups before we regulate, and one of the most important fields where we feel that regulations can be made more cost effective and beneficial to Canadians as a whole, is in the area
of creating parliamentary accountability. Our task force, as well as that as that of the joint standing committee and the economic council, indicated that parliamentarians had a paramount role to play in holding regulators accountable. This is why we called for the creation of a special task force which could deal with a review of regulations on their merit as well as the whole process of implementing regulatory reform. We want to see the day when committees from this House consisting of members from all sides can work in non-partisan fashion with expert staff and thus serve their constituents better by having the capability of dealing with regulations.
We do not want to create a roadblock in this House. We do not want committees to have the opportunity of holding up further the process of this House of Commons through technical rules, such as creating a debate on a report of every committee. We would be further hamstrung and, goodness knows, the Canadian public knows that we do not have the time in this House at present to deal at length with all the issues which we feel are of a pressing and urgent nature. We feel the House itself could be relieved of many of those responsibilities by adequately staffed, adequately equipped, small committees.
We are calling for committee reform of all the standing committees so that members can devote their expertise and time to probably one committee only. By doing this, members can get into the substance of matters. Political partisanship would never disappear but it would give way to enlightened consideration of the laws that we seek to implement for the good of all Canadians.
That is the type of process we have been talking about. Abusing the rules of this House will not permit us to get on with it. What I am happy so say, however, is that not only did our task force have the opinion, the opportunity and the consideration of hon. members who formed part of the standing joint committee, but we also had the benefit of their excellent work in the area of regulatory reform. Even though we tabled the report last December 19, we have not moved concurrence in it because we have had the assurance of our hon. House leader and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) that the consideration of our report as well as other reports in this area were being taken into consideration and acted upon.
I am very proud to be a member of a government which, under the actions of our President of the Privy Council, has undertaken a 12-point program to implement the reforms of which we speak. We do not need to grandstand in this House to get our reforms implemented and considered, nor does the standing joint committee. Those reforms are being implemented and looked at.
I would like to refer the House to the 12 points of reform that have been implemented and are under review by the President of the Privy Council.

Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
the CTC, has decided not to ask. It simply proceeded on its own.

speechtext:
I am pleased to know that the chairman of the committee agrees with the statement.
I would like to discuss some of the concerns expressed to me by my constituents as a result of the announcement of July 27. There has always been friction between my part of the country and central Canada because our population is in the minority. Several constituents have approached me and suggested that the reason for the cutbacks was that obviously there was not enough money to go around, that if anyone was to be shortchanged it would not be the central part of the country but the west or the maritimes, and that the real reason for the cutbacks was not necessarily that the government wanted to save money but that it wanted to provide better service to central Canada, Ontario and Quebec, on the Quebec City to Windsor corridor.
Evidence of this was pointed out to me. It is, as we know by the minister's admission, that the new light, rapid and comfortable trains which are coming onstream-they will be delayed by a month which, in some cases, is understandable- will not be used in western Canada. This was pointed out as an example of how the cutbacks would hurt my part of the country and benefit the central part. I am sure maritime members would relate it to their part of the country. To some extent I am guilty of the same kind of prejudice, but what really is the case is that all parts of the country will be affected, not only the west and the maritimes but also the central part of the country. It seems to me that that is shortchanging Canadians and pitting Canadian against Canadian unnecessarily.

If the Canadian Transport Commission had been given a mandate to hold hearings and had travelled across the country and heard Canadians' complaints, as did the task force our party set up, this would have become very much more obvious, and I think the media, including the press, would have picked up the fact that cutbacks were occurring right across the country. Canadians would have had a better chance to understand why these cuts were taking place, and they would have had less reason to blame other parts of the country for their own deprivation as far as rail passenger service is concerned. I think that is a very important point as far as national unity is concerned at this time. I do not think we need to do anything that in any way suggests that one part of the country is benefiting at the expense of another. Yet by not holding hearings, that is precisely what this government is allowing to happen.
As I said, I think to some extent I am as guilty as others. I appeared before the task force when it held its hearings in Winnipeg and made statements to that effect. I was very quickly corrected. I realize that was a bad mistake on my part, but again I say that the process by which this decision was reached lends itself to that kind of misinformation. That does not do any of us in this country a service. I think that is a very important reason, if there is no other reason, that the government should have given the Canadian Transport Commission a mandate to hold hearings and to talk about why rail passenger service had to be cut as far as some parts of the country are concerned. I put that out because I have not heard anyone else make that point. I think it is a very valid point which needs to be made, emphasized and understood by the government.
Many points have been made by my constituents, one of them being that my constituents did not think VIA Rail had been in existence long enough to develop the kind of usage it needed in order to be viable. Many people told me that they would be willing to pay considerably more-some people said two times or even three times as much as the present fare structure-if they could have a chance to have the service maintained. I suppose it is easy for people to say that if they think the service will be discontinued. I suppose it is easy to say that they would be willing to pay more because they know, at least by all intents, that the service will not be there and that their bluff with respect to paying more will not be called. However, the point is that they were not given that kind of opportunity.
I and many of my constituents would like to have seen VIA Rail management come out and say the service was losing money and needed a year or two in which to try a new marketing policy and would increase fares in order to cut some of its losses. If, after a period of new management and new ideas with respect to increasing revenues, VIA was still in the hole and thought it could save the $100 million to which the minister refers, then the cuts could be made. In that case people would have felt better. They would have known that they had had a chance to support the service. If, after a year or two, or whatever the appropriate time would be, the service was still losing money, the people would have known that they
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
had had a chance and that there was not enough activity to support the level of passenger service which there had been in the past.
When we consider the routes which were abandoned, we really have to question why some of the decisions were made. The trip from Winnipeg to Vancouver takes one through Portage la Prairie, Brandon, Regina and Calgary. That is the main line of the CPR. It parallels the Trans-Canada highway to a large extent. On a good highway like the Trans-Canada there is obviously good bus service and good highway service. That implies that people who are close to that highway are able to travel.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: They have options.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Exactly, but that was not the route that was abandoned. The government abandoned the CN route which, beyond Portage la Prairie, goes through areas which are not at all close to a good highway, and those areas are left virtually without service. The valid question posed to me is that if the government is going to abandon one of the trans-continental routes, why not the CP route? After all, CP is the company which has done everything it could in the last 15 years to discourage passenger service. At least over the past 15 years CN has tried something. CN had its "red, white and blue days." It has tried to attract people to its trains, yet the CN route is the one which will be abandoned after November 15.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: They will be black and blue days.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My friend, the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid), points out that the days will not be red, white and blue any more; they will be black and blue as far as the citizens of the country are concerned. The citizens are being abused in relation to the transportation services they have been used to.
Once we get away from the proper process-I argue very strongly that doing so is detrimental in many ways-we really have to question why the decision was made the way it was. That leads me back to the process. If we had gone through the proper process which, I argue, is by way of the CTC, we would have had a chance to see some of the alternatives which perhaps might have worked. We probably would have had a chance to arrive at a better decision on providing transportation for Canadians.
The hon. member for Willowdale stood up and piously talked about all the good things he wants to see in terms of reform of the House of Commons, but at the same time he supported a blatant cut in service which he and his government have a chance to refer to the CTC. How somebody can be so sincere and yet so inconsistent just boggles the mind.
Another great concern to Canadians is that abandoning a service such as this cannot be done properly in four or five months. We had a chance to speak to the bus industry when the Transport Committee travelled to the province of Quebec in the month of September. Representatives of that industry pointed out to us that VIA Rail held absolutely no consulta-

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments tions with the bus industry. To a large extent, the bus industry of Canada pays its own way. Hon. members can argue about the subsidies which accrue to the bus industry through taxes to finance highways, but the industry does not receive any of the direct subsidies that VIA Rail receives.
VIA Rail has talked about the number of passengers it carries increasing but, when we consider the way people in Canada travel, it becomes obvious that the major portion of this increase in the number of passengers will be people who use buses. The bus industry has cross-subsidization. The industry makes money on some of its main routes, such as the Quebec City-Windsor route, and uses that money to operate routes to smaller towns. I understand that Ontario and Quebec are the best examples of provinces where that cross-subsidization occurs. The bus industry is saying that if we take away its main revenue generating routes by attracting passengers to the Quebec City-Windsor rail route, there will not be enough money to support some of the routes on which the bus industry is losing, those routes being to smaller centres in Ontario and Quebec.
That does not do anything in terms of providing increased transportation for Canadians. Even if the government has decided to abandon many rail passenger routes, it would make good sense to do it over a period of a year or two so that the bus industry will have a chance to gear up to take some of the additional passengers who previously travelled by rail.
The bus companies point out very correctly that they cannot go out and buy buses in the same way one goes to a corner store to buy a quart of milk. It is a major expenditure to buy a bus to provide additional service. Bus companies need time in which to do this. By acting arbitrarily and on such short notice, the government has shown that it has no sensitivity or any feeling at all with respect to the demands which will be made on the bus industry.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: The government does not care.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Furthermore, I suppose the lesson in this is that the government does not care.
In my province the railways were the real reason for the coming into existence of many small communities. That happened about 100 years ago. During the summers of 1982 and 1983 there will be celebrations in many large and small communities. Brandon, a city of 40,000, will have its one hundredth anniversary very soon. Those communities came into existence because of the railroads. Without them they would not be in existence. It has been pointed out to me many times that it is ironic that this government is taking part in those celebrations by removing the rail service. Many people resent that. They resent the fact that the rail service will be gone, but they resent just as much the fact that it will be gone without any reference to the proper regulatory body, that being the Canadian Transport Commission. I fail to understand why the government is so afraid of referring this whole matter to the Canadian Transport Commission. This brings me back to the motion before us this afternoon. I think
everyone agrees it would make a lot of sense to have a VIA Rail act.
We have a Crown corporation spending literally hundreds of millions of dollars. It is committed to spending those dollars each succeeding year over a number of years. I suppose it really amounts to billions of dollars over a period of a few years.
I cannot understand why we do not have a VIA Rail act which sets out the objectives of VIA Rail, what it hopes to accomplish, the mandate it should have, and how the government should assist it in performing that mandate or whether the government expects VIA Rail to finance itself totally from the marketplace.
We do not have that kind of act. The minister says he has a draft of the act. It is a major operation for any government department to draft an act. It is a complete waste of the time of the bureaucracy to have an act in some kind of preliminary draft and not be willing to bring the act before the House of Commons where we can properly debate and develop it.
The chairman of VIA Rail is in favour of a VIA Rail act. I would be surprised if either of the railroads was against it. We would know then where we stand in terms of passenger service for this country. VIA Rail would have a yardstick against which to measure its performance. It would know what kind of mandate it had from this government and this Parliament. However, the government is very reluctant to do that.
We talk about energy costs. We just reached an energy-pricing agreement in this country that will double gasoline and diesel fuel prices in the next three or four years. We do not know whether two or three years down the road energy prices will be so steep that people will leave their private automobiles, buses and airlines for the efficiency of a train.
The hon. member for Vegreville spoke of this earlier. I do not want to belabour it, but it is a point worth repeating. Until we have a definite idea of the efficiency of railroads in terms of energy use in moving a person one mile or 100 miles, we do not know whether or not we are getting rid of a very efficient method of moving people in this country.
In western Canada the distances are very great. Therefore, in many cases the people have become accustomed to using the railroad and have become dependent on it. I was in St. Lazare the day after the cut there was announced. It is a small community of 300 or 400 people. VIA Rail stopped there. I spoke to some of the merchants in St. Lazare. They told me that people came regularly from 100 miles away to get the train for Vancouver or eastern Canada. If the rail service there is removed, these people will have to drive another 100 miles to reach the railroad. That community will be hurt as far as attracting business is concerned.
Within the past two or three years, a station was built there which has the proprer facilities for handling passengers. If the passenger service is taken away, that facility will be of no use. It makes no sense to abandon on November 15 what the
October 26, 1981

minister is proposing without hearing the complaints and concerns of the people there.
Another valid suggestion made to me was that rather than remove the whole service from the northern route, the CN route, it should be alternated, one day on the CP line through Regina and Calgary and the other day through Saskatoon and Edmonton. It will still be necessary to maintain the stations in Edmonton and Saskatoon. We are told that there will still be service between Winnipeg and Saskatoon but it will be diverted through Regina. Therefore, we must still maintain the stations. Why not have alternate service? I wonder why the government has not considered some of these matters.
In closing, I very much hope that this motion will be adopted today. We will see how sincere the pious words of the hon. member for Willowdale are when he votes on the motion, or whether the government will decide it should be talked out. I wonder whether the reason we are having this debate is that the government does not have enough members here to win the vote and therefore it is afraid of a vote. Perhaps that is why we are being given this opportunity to debate VIA Rail. For whatever reason, and maybe it is the only reason, we are pleased to have this debate. I hope the government will concur in this motion and bring forth a VIA Rail act very soon so that VIA Rail will have a proper mandate and will not only provide but increase passenger service to Canadians.

So, Mr. Speaker, this is a list of municipalities representing people of my riding, and this does not include all the letters I received from constituents who cannot believe the minister

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments would make such a decision at this time. Today, I was looking up in parliamentary records what a member of this House, the member for Chapleau, said in 1946 during the throne speech debate, on March 26, 1946. The member, Mr. Speaker, who happened to be my grandfather, said, and I quote:
In passing, I take the occasion of suggesting to the directors of the Canadian National Railways that it is high time to improve the railway line which runs through our district if they want to furnish travellers with suitable means of transportation as well as take care of the shipping demand arising from the various products I have just listed.
Strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, 35 years later, I seem to be in the same situation as my grandfather who was then member for Chapleau, and I could quote a number of speeches where he fought against exactly the same problem I am faced with today, that is, changes in the system of transportation in my riding. Last week, my colleague, the member for La Prairie (Mr. Deniger) told the House that what they were doing was cutting off deadwood to make the tree more vigorous. Well, I would like to say to my hon. colleague that what they are doing is cutting the roots, and then there will be no tree, no essential transportation service-the keyword is essential-left for the people. We have heard opposition members mainly the transport critic, and where was this same transport critic when the opposition was in power?
I am convinced that the department is now continuing a policy which was probably initiated by our opponents. With his leader, the former Minister of Transport was probably much too busy moving embassies around to be concerned with flights from Dorval to Mirabel. He probably initiated the policy that the department is now implementing. I am against this policy, Mr. Speaker, and as the various statements and resolutions that I have mentioned show, the people are not only behind me, but also with me, and support my work in this House.
Yesterday, I held a meeting of the Association in my constituency. About 100 people came to tell me that to cut back a service which is essential to an aging population-I do not want to repeat the speech that I made last week, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that this service can simply not disappear. I therefore ask the minister, through you, to please review this policy and, if possible, not to abandon completely the service in the constituency of Argenteuil-Papineau, but perhaps simply reduce it. I believe that even this will satisfy the population.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that it would be to the advantage of VIA Rail to re-examine its evaluation policy. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that it would be to its advantage at the very least to consult the people to know what are the best times to travel in the constituency. I have received the following telegram, which is self-explanatory:
Dear Sir,
In accordance with the proposal sent to you by the Laurentian region on October 16, 1981, concerning the maintenance and improvement of the passenger services on . . . the Montreal-Lachute-Ottawa line. The Association touris-tique des Laurentides and the Conseil regional de developpement des Laurentides ask all of you ... to support the motion . . . introduced-
-by my colleague from Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). I replied of course, that if it had carried, this motion would have resulted in the fall of the government. This is why I had to support the government. Mr. Speaker, groups such as those and such as the Conseil regional de developpement de l'Ou-taouais, and telegrams such as this one from the Canadian Railway Labour Association:
The Canadian Railway Labour Association on behalf of all railway workers in Canada particularly the members of the CBRT and GW urges you to support the Conservative motion concerning the proposed VIA Rail cutbacks.

Well, I am saying to those groups that their lobby, much like today's, that is forcing Canadians to pay for travelling expenses-I suggest that the official opposition could have used another much more effective means.

speechtext:
I realize that my colleague opposite is using a language which is not altogether parliamentary, but since he does not have full command of Moliere's language I will disregard that accusation.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, to my mind it is quite normal that, 35 years after another one, a member stands up in the House to fight against exactly the same thing as did my grandfather, then member for Chapleau, in the debate in reply to the Speech from the Throne on March 20, 1946. It will be impossible for me to repeat it often enough, Mr. Speaker, and I am now asking myself this question: Is it true that the more things change the more they remain the same? I see that the opposition is resorting to more or less effective means. Again I repeat that it is false to say that Liberal members on this side have been gagged. I have not been gagged and I was very severe and very hard with a minister of my government. But, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that within the near future the minister will review his policy and then formally deny all the allegations made by the opposition. As I was saying, I fail to understand why the minister should have implemented that policy. Rather I believed that the transport critic, the former minister, was the instigator of that policy.
There is another phenomenon, Mr. Speaker, and I refer to the transfer of flights from Dorval to Mirabel. I said last week that we have waited much too long in that field. We are now letting the situation go to pot and if it is not quickly corrected everything will have been damaged beyond repair. Mr. Speaker, it is urgent that the Department of Transport make a decision about transferring flights from Dorval to Mirabel so as to prevent what is called Canada's largest airport from becoming a huge white elephant. True enough, it is now a huge white elephant, but I am convinced that with the good will of the government we will soon have the largest airport in
October 26, 1981

Canada, one which was built by a Liberal government and which will be developed by a Liberal government.
Where was the former Minister of Transport? They were too concerned, during their short stay in power, as I said earlier, with moving embassies around to make decisions about the Department of Transport.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the minister will review his position and that the people of Argenteuil will have a new train service. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, in view of all the facts I put forward, of the support of municipalities-
I am certain the government will not let the people down, that it will have to do something for the only remaining railway line in the Ottawa Valley, for the only rail service on the Quebec North Shore, and therefore I ask, once again, through you, Mr. Speaker, that a review be undertaken, or that at least hearings be held so that the people can be heard.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to take part in this debate, and I can assure you that I will give the people of my riding cause to be satisfied with the work done by their Member of Parliament.
