The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has the floor.
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is now in the House and I know that he has had a busy day but I hope that he will take part in the debate between now and ten o'clock tonight.
I support the motion for concurrence in the seventh report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, which is an all-party report from both Houses. I want to deal with the major part of paragraph 4 of the report and some parts of paragraph 5. First of all, I should like to thank the regular members of the committee and the co-chairmen for the courtesy they showed in hearing me out and accepting my suggestion for an amendment to the report when it was being discussed.
In paragraph 4 of the report, the following statement appears:
In your committee's judgment, the settling of the legal regime to govern the now publicly owned, controlled and funded railway passenger service is too important a matter to be left to the corporate policy, and virtually unlimited corporate powers, of VIA Rail Canada Inc., a corporation wholly owned by the Crown, and to skeletal regulations made under a dollar vote which in the nature of procedure in the House of Commons cannot have been subjected to significant debate. Parliament should have been, and still should be, given the opportunity to debate the future and structure of railway passenger services in Canada and the manner of their management and control-
I want to thank the committee again for accepting my representation. The paragraph continues:
-and your committee is inclined to believe that this should include the maintenance of the jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission over VIA Rail Canada.
The order in council that the minister used to wipe out these passenger routes, overrides and reverses 15 decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission, which ordered that those 15 routes be retained. In paragraph 5 of the report there appears the following:
It may be that your committee has been too patient in seeking assurances from the Minister of Transport that a bill to regularize VIA Rail Canada Inc.'s activities and powers would be introduced. Indications of the preparation of such a bill were received but lately it has become apparent that legislative action has become a retreating vision.
I invite you, Mr. Speaker, and all hon. members to read the exchange of letters between the minister and the co-chairmen of the committee. His first two responses were to the effect, "It is coming any day". The last response was that it did not seem to be needed nor was it necessary at the moment. This report was unanimously adopted by all parties in both Houses of Parliament, so it is not to be taken lightly.
Under the program proposed by the minister and his bureaucrats, the 99.8 per cent sold-out sleeping cars of the Canadian Pacific's "Canadian" run will offer the only full service train across Canada to the west coast, and the 99.5 per cent sold-out sleeping car accommodation on the CNR Supercontinental will be chopped. This is using data issued in July, 1981. In fact, what will remain will be a partial "day at a time" coach or dayliner, with no service offered, on the most heavily patronized part of the Supercontinental route, the Edmonton-Jasper-Vancouver portion. A dayliner will be run from Winnipeg to Regina and up to Saskatoon, and it is

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
suggested that one will be run from Saskatoon to Edmonton. That is supposed to be some kind of alternative.
Before the supper hour, the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) spoke about the abuse of the rules when the opposition moves concurrence of a report of a committee of the Elouse. I do not have the exact figures here but I have talked to some colleagues and to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and it appears that out of 103 or 105 or 107 reports submitted to this House, the opposition has moved concurrence in three. If that is an abuse, then surely it is drawing a long bow. In fact, it could reasonably be claimed by members of the government that the opposition has been derelict in its duty in not calling for concurrence of more reports. I think there have been a number of times when we should have and did not. There is no one in this government or in previous ones, no matter which party was in power, who can claim that the opposition overuses or abuses the procedure of calling for concurrence of a committee report or calling for a debate. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker.
I want to go on now to another area which concerns respect for, regard of, consideration of and consultation with the statutes of legislatures in Canada. Where does the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) stand on this whole issue? Where does the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne), the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley) or the hon. member who just spoke, stand on it? There are at least 21 members on the government side, and if all of them told the minister that he had to change his decision or they would not support him, then the minister would have to do that. Would they be willing to do this at their Wednesday caucus? The remedy does not lie in the hands of the opposition, Mr. Speaker.
Scores of people came here today from Atlantic Canada and western Canada to plead with the minister but he turned them down. In total, those people represent something like three million Canadians. The person who came from the city council of Edmonton had been instructed on behalf of that council, which represents over half a million people. The mayor of the town of Melville was also instructed; he represents 6,000 people. The three score or four score or five score people who came here today did not come as a mass delegation; they came as instructed delegates, representatives of over three million Canadians, to ask the Minister of Transport to reconsider, to delay, if not to rescind, this order. They ask that for a number of reasons and I want to cite some of these reasons, which I hope the minister and his legal counsel will consider. I want to ask the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mr. Gourd) who just spoke whether he would care to check the statutes of the province of Quebec-of 1882, would you believe? That was an agreement between the government of Quebec of that day and what was then called the Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa and Occidental Railway Company. When Canadian Pacific took over that route in 1882, the Quebec statute stated:
The said Canadian Pacific Railway hereby bind themselves to maintain the said road in good repair, and to run the same regularly and efficiently with a
sufficient number of trains every day to carry the freight and passenger traffic with due regularity and despatch, running at least one passenger train every day each way.
I hope the hon. member for London East will have something to say about this statutory obligation in the Quebec statutes. It was assumed by Canadian Pacific and subsequently assumed by VIA Rail.
Let us turn to British Columbia. The British Columbia statutes of 1910 related to the Canadian Northern Railway. In return for certain acreages of land and timber rights, the Canadian Northern agreed to certain conditions required by statute in British Columbia. I quote from page 1910 of the Canadian Northern Agreement as follows:
The Northern Company agrees that the Pacific Company will, from and after the completion of the mainland line ... cause to be maintained, a regular daily first-class passenger and freight service between a harbour at or near the city of Victoria and the system of the Northern Company lying to the east of the province of British Columbia-
What is meant is that the line which runs from Vancouver to Jasper was agreed to in 1910 and was to be maintained as a daily, first-class passenger service. Canadian Northern went bankrupt in spite of all the acreage and timber rights it had. It was taken over by Canadian National in 1919 or 1920.
The Canadian National Railways Act in no way obviates the statutes of British Columbia in 1910. In fact, Canadian National assumed the statutory obligation of Canadian Northern to run a daily passenger train between Vancouver and Jasper. Surely it follows quite logically that VIA Rail, established to bail CP and CN out of their legal liabilities for hauling people, also assumed that statutory obligation.
If the provincial statutes are not sufficient to convince the Minister of Transport and his cabinet colleagues, let us look at federal statutes. Section 12 of the federal statute of 1890 relating to the Montreal and Western Railway Company stated:
The Pacific Company-
That means CPR.
-will, during the said term, provide and run over the said railway duly equipped trains for the carriage of passengers and freight as frequently as shall be necessary for the traffic of the country-
It goes on to state:
-the Pacific Company will run during summer months at least one train carrying passengers each way on every business day; and during the rest of the year at least one such train one way on every business day;-
That is the federal statute of 1890, chapter 67, relating to the line that the Minister of Transport has ordered abandoned, running from Montreal to Hull and Ottawa.
Of course, there is a clause in the National Transportation Act that says the minister can amend, vary or rescind an order of the Canadian Transport Commission.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: That's right, but not the statutes.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is in there for an excellent reason. When the National Transportation Act was passed in 1966-67, the tradition in those days was that the CTC, the old board of railway commissioners, only held a hearing at the request of
October 26, 1981

the railroads or the government, and the public be damned. The public could not get a hearing. The Parliament of that day, and hon. members on all sides of the House said, "In a case where the CTC does not pay any attention to the public or does not even give them a chance, we want some way in which the government of the day could overrule it on behalf of the public interest." Section 64 was then put in the act. The desire of Parliament and the public was for the section to be used in that limited manner.
Subsequent to that passage of legislation, various ministers of transport have used that section to rescind, vary, modify or amend one decision of the CTC, which is only relatively recent, being six months old or a year old. However, this minister is not only taking the chicken out of the coop but has stolen the whole coop. He has rescinded 15 orders of the Canadian Transport Commission, the oldest of which goes back to 1975 or 1976.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: 1 defy the minister or anyone else to try to maintain in this Parliament that that was the intent of Parliament or that it was the spirit of the legislation. Therefore, the minister has flown in the face of statutory requirements of two provinces that we have been able to dig up so far-and we are going back into some more stuff-and one statute of the federal Parliament of Canada, and has violated the spirit and the intent of the National Transportation Act, namely, Section 64, upon which he relies. Not even his predecessor, who had a lot of gall, would have had the gall to do this.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who was he?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In fact, he is making the former minister of transport, Otto Lang, look good.
The minister is lecturing us today about the romantics who want to talk about keeping railway passenger trains. I want to tell the minister that there happen to be a few people around this country who know a lot more about public transportation than he will ever know. I want to tell the minister that he had better start listening to those people. If he does not want to listen to them, perhaps he can listen to people from other countries in the world who know a lot more about it than he does.
It is the wrong decision. It is wrong in terms of transportation economics, it is wrong in terms of transportation efficiency, it is wrong in terms of safety, it is wrong in terms of the environment, and it is wrong in terms of the trend all over the industrialized world, and even in some underdeveloped countries. In fact, Your Honour may have noticed an article in the paper the other day which stated that the CPR received a $54 million contract to build a railroad in Malaysia. Why do we not give it one to rebuild the railroad in Canada?
This report must be concurred in. I congratulate the committee. I hope, and I have reason to believe, that in a subsequent report the committee will come up with even better arguments than it has in this one, and the ones it has in this
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
one are excellent. I hope the House will concur in this report. I hope the minister will have the courage to rise and agree that if it should not be rescinded, at least the decision he has made should be substantially delayed, and we will bless him for it.

speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to listen to the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mr. Gourd). He talked about his grandfather who had made a representation in 1946 to the Government of Canada that it was backing away from civic responsibility in the provision of rail and passenger service. Today the grandson, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau, is making representations on behalf of his own constituents along the same line. I sincerely hope he will have the success he deserves because he voted for the cancellation of the present services and against the delay of that order of cabinet passed so highhandedly and without consideration of the needs of people.
The hon. member accused us of being rather partisan in our presentation. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you know, that the motion was not a motion of non-confidence when we introduced it for discussion last week. It was clearly stated by us and by the New Democratic Party that we would be happy to allow with unanimous consent, that it was not a motion of non-confidence. We have had enough drivel and lip service from Liberals. Let us level with our constituents for a change instead of trying to whip-saw both sides of the issues, one against the other.
1 was pretty impressed by the speech made by hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) this afternoon. He made a great speech on behalf of more definitive legislation and less regulation. He stated in his high-toned speech that yes, the minister was justified in exercising ministerial authority over and above traditional and historic practice and the intention of the National Transportation Act to cancel 20 per cent of VIA Rail. You cannot have it coming and going and at the same time be sincere. I ask to the hon. member, which way does he want it? Does he want regulation; does he want ministerial authority? I ask him again, which one does he want? Does he want government by legislation, regulation or ministerial authority? It cannot be both ways. I wonder how the hon. member for Willowdale will vote on Bill C-48. After the sanctimonious speech he made, he sort of backed himself into a corner by saying that he could not vote for Bill C-48 because, in effect, it is a bill of regulation and an extension of government athority to ministerial discretion. Which way is the hon. member going to go? If he called himself a liar, it would not be out of order, would it?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN REVISED SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall retract that. In any event, if he contradicts himself in any vote on Bill C-48 which extends regulatory or ministerial discretion, then his speech of today,

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments which was intended to be high-toned in the main, will have become of no consequence. That is the kind of debate that is taking place.
I want to come back to the subject of New Brunswick for a minute. The other night as I sat here in the Elouse, I could not help thinking about the Mother Goose rhyme about the seven little blackbirds who sat in a tree, or seven little puppets who sat on a limb, and one fell off and then there were six. I noticed that as we voted, one had fallen off. That was the hon. member for Saint John (Mr. Landers).
Now I come to the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin). He abstained totally from any responsibility to his constituents, a responsibility which they expected of him. According to rumour, he did it, first, on being approached and asked to the objections to support rail cancellations and to represent his constituency so as to prevent the cancellation of the line from his home town or city, whichever the case may be, the route from Edmundston to Moncton. His response was, "The government has done it. It has to be right, and I have to support it," and, "No, I cannot make those representations". That is the rumour. I did not see that in print. I did not hear him say those words, but there was a report along those lines. That part of New Brunswick got the usual service from the Liberal Party of Canada. When he was needed and when our interests needed protection, he voted with the government of which he was a member.
We can now turn to the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail). 1 would like to reflect for a while on Section 64 of the National Transportation Act. Everyone refers to it but I wonder if someone has bothered to read it into the record. I will do so to show you once again that the government is right in using it to proceed with this rationalization measure. Subsection (1) of Section 64 says, and I quote:
The Governor in Council may at any time, in his descretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion-
-of his own motion-
-and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the Commission, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the Governernor in Council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the Commission and upon all parties.
There is a lot of fancy footwork being done to try to prove that there is a difference between a cabinet decision, an order in council that amends a single decision of the CTC and one that varies several decisions. The act makes no such distinction. Section 64 of the National Transportation Act applies to both the plural and the singular. So we should read this before accusing the government of legal indecency in its use of Section 64. What we have to ask ourselves is why Section 64 was included in the National Transportation Act. It is simple. In some cases, we can refer to the CTC to find out if a line is economical, if it is viable in the public interest, whether or not it should be maintained. But in some cases, it is the entire system which is in question. In some instances, the government wonders not if such and such line should be reviewed, but whether the entire system should not be reconsidered. And the act of 1967, in particular Section 64(1), gives the government the power to change the whole system and that is precisely what we are doing now.

Finally, 1 would have had to tell the Canadian Transport Commission that, as it has said so itself in the past, commuter transportation is basically a provincial and urban responsibility. Why? Because the kind of work to be done, that is, combining subway lines, buses and railways, must be done by local authorities. Well, that is exactly what we are doing now. I would have had to tell the Canadian Transport Commission: Do what the government is doing now. And my friends in the official opposition would have said once again that not only was I an imperialist, but I was a hypocrite as well. So now, at least, I am not called a hypocrite. Thank God for small blessings.
Since the beginning of this debate, the official opposition has been saying: Listen, why don't you postpone this. interfere in the evolution of transportation policy by changing the terms of reference and by creating a climate of uncertainty and a lack of predictability so that it would be virtually impossible to manage a corporation such as VIA Rail. We need a VIA Rail act to establish clearly the basis on which the railways will charge VIA Rail for running rights and the use of equipment. In other words, we need a reconstitution of costing order R63-13. We also need to know where rail transportation will fit in our scale of national transportation priorities. It is not enough for the minister to stand in this House, Mr. Speaker, and wax eloquent about the days of the blacksmith and the four revolutions in the history of transportation and about the fact that his father worked on the railroad. All of that, Mr. Speaker, suggests that the Minister of Transport has a preconceived disposition to end passenger rail service in Canada. I think this is quite clear if you read between the lines of everything he says. He is saying that in the future in this country we are going to travel in airplanes or stuffed into buses over distances of four or six hundred miles, and that includes the elderly, the handicapped people and others who do not find it convenient or comfortable nor, in fact, conducive to their state of health to travel by other means than rail.
We need to know the extent to which the government and Parliament will consider the importance of our national rail passenger system to our economy, Mr. Speaker. That brings in specifically the question of tourism and the importance of tourism and of attracting people from all parts of the world, from the Pacific rim, Europe and the United States of America and elsewhere, to come and enjoy our country and partake of our beautiful scenery, and thus bring important economic benefits to thousands of businesses across Canada, whether they be hotel businesses, restaurants, car rental operations, ski package promoters or any of the large businesses and host of individuals who operate those businesses to earn a livelihood.
The VIA Rail Act must be undertaken with due regard for the importance of rail transportation to our economy. Of course, we have to embark on this initiative, given a full and thorough debate of the question of energy and the relative costs of various types of transportation. It is far too easy, Mr. Speaker, to adopt things by the back door and pretend they have the facts to back up the decisions they take when, in fact, those facts are distorted, misleading and selectively chosen to substantiate a biased case, Mr. Speaker.
I thought the minister was going to challenge that comment. But in fact he knows, Mr. Speaker, he is on very shaky grounds. In fact, in this House he has admitted he is really not much of an expert with numbers. This is a numbers game, Mr. Speaker, where the minister cannot merely resort to the inferences and selectively chosen statistics that some of his senior officials are apparently putting in front of him. We must know the means by which the VIA Rail corporation will be required to report to Parliament and to the standing committee, and what their relationship will be with the Canadian Transport Commission in terms of policies and regulations affecting the

October 26, 1981
Regulations and other Statutory Instruments
provisions of services which were originally undertaken as a commitment by those national rail systems that have provided passenger service for the most part of a century.
Those obligations have never been rescinded. It is important to know the extent to which VIA Rail will be required to continue those obligations and provide perpetual rail services, or some altered form of it, in accordance with the needs of public good, and public necessity and public convenience, which is what the Canadian Transport Commission is mandated to determine.
Before we pass this VIA Rail act, Mr. Speaker, we must know what the obligation of VIA Rail is going to be to its employees, members of the various railway brotherhoods and operating unions, some of whom became members of a new union with the expectation of a whole career with VIA Rail ahead of them. They relinquished their seniority in the unions they had belonged to earlier. They fully trusted and expected the government to guarantee them a rewarding and remunerative career with VIA Rail.
The back door, moonlighting actions the minister has taken this past summer essentially break a trust with these employees who felt they would have a career with the national railway company. But instead, the minister says, "That is all right, we will take care of them. We are going to pay them off. We are going to put them into early retirement or send them somewhere down to central Canada so they can be retrained to pass sandwiches on an LRC train running between Quebec City and Windsor". That is not good enough for people who have given their whole career to the railway and who have learned a trade in the service of the passenger rail system of our country.
We need to incorporate within the VIA Rail act a clear obligation and undertaking to those who would be employed by that corporation in the service of our people. We have to set out clearly a provision for reporting on the finances of this corporation. A clear distinction has to be drawn between the capital budgeting for new equipment so that we can actually put aside, on a year by year basis, a steady flow of capital funding instead of having these fits and bursts of capital as was the case 25 years ago when we bought a lot of new rail equipment. Then we did not buy anything again for 25 years.
A railway cannot plan and build a modern system using modern equipment if it cannot have a properly laid out system of capital budgeting and planning for the expansion of that service. It cannot watch its budget being subjected to the meat axe at every whim of the politicians to save a few dollars.
We must know what the nature of the operating budget of this corporation is going to be. We have to know to what extent the railways will be able to overcharge for fixed costs, whether or not the passenger trains are running. We have to know to what extent the railways want to charge for rail grinding and resurfacing-which is necessary-largely due to the heavy unit trains that are using our rails and to what extent VIA Rail is being expected to pay excessive charges that are incurred because of other traffic on those rails.
We want to know how much fuel VIA Rail is using. I have tried to do some energy calculations in order to determine that. It is very convenient for the minister that this information is not available. Presumably the railways charge VIA in bulk for all the fuel it uses. It is very difficult to determine how many energy units of fuel are actually being burned in moving passengers, as compared with the movement of the freight and bulk materials. We require a proper accounting and reporting procedure so that the officials of VIA Rail know that they will not be hosed, to put it frankly, by the national rail systems which provide the rights-of-way on which it operates.
We require a procedure of reporting on performance. For example, we must know what means we will use to decide when a particular line or a particular service is so marginal that it should be discontinued. The rules must be put up front. We should know whether we are prepared to subsidize, for example, 50 per cent of the operating costs of a line, and not one cent more, as is the case with the Amtrak system. If we believe the rail system should be serving the social needs of people in the remote and less populated areas of Canada, then we must accept the concept of subsidy, which is just another way of having taxpayers pay for the service in any event. It is not the government which is paying for these things. It is taxpayers, and the priority should be determined by taxpayers. It should be very clear in the VIA Rail act the extent to which passenger rail services will serve the national interest, not merely the dollar and cents interests of the government which wants to buy some new LRC trains so that it can conveniently cut the services which the people in the more remote and rural areas of the country clearly need. We require all of this information before Parliament can debate it in the context of evolving a VIA Rail act.
It took the minister only 30 minutes to make the decisions which he enacted on July 27. To come into the House and tell us that it will somehow take five years, is really an insult to the House. If we merely resolve to adopt as an element of our national transportation policy the philosophy that passenger rail trains will continue in Canada, given the experience in other countries and the fact that we know passenger trains are cheaper in terms of energy consumption than any other form of transportation, we should get on with creating a system which grows, works and serves the needs of all Canadians.
I should like to talk for a moment about the credibility of information. The minister justified his actions by saying that trains are inefficient, the least energy efficient of all transportation methods. Of course this is pure rubbish. It is just not true. The minister is trying to suggest that there are not enough people using these trains as a reason for not continuing them. In fact, the statistics show otherwise. It is a matter of whom he is directing his questions to. To make superficial, simple-minded statements to the effect that railways are one of the least energy efficient of all transportation modes is just absolute "sluttergush". The minister is misleading the House, perhaps unintentionally, by suggesting that he is qualified to decide on the relative merits of rail service compared with air

transportation and other modes, which we know are heavily subsidized by the taxpayers by one means or another.
The statistics on national trends and cost recovery prepared by the minister's department show that in 1977 there was only a 32 per cent cost recovery for the provision of air transportation services in Canada, a 22 per cent cost recovery on marine services, and a 49 per cent cost recovery on the highway system which serves passenger cars, buses and highway transport trucks. In comparison, the railways are operating with an 82 per cent cost recovery. Granted, much of that high rate of return on the rails is because of the carriage of freight, but surely it is not too much to ask that some of the excess earnings, far in excess of the earnings in the other three modes, be redirected to guarantee convenient, comfortable rail transportation services for all Canadians.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-POSSIBLE POSTPONEMENT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
THE CONSTITUTION-POSSIBLE POSTPONEMENT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 20, 1981, in this House, 1 asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether he still intended to renew his invitation to the provinces after their repeated refusals to hold a federal-provincial meeting on the constitutional resolution.
It will be remembered that such an invitation had repeatedly been extended by the Prime Minister but had always been turned down by the premiers under various pretences. Finally, the provinces, after a meeting held on October 19, 1981, in Montreal, agreed to such a meeting to be held in the first week of November. Whether this was a tactical move is open to question, since the presentation of the federal budget had already been announced for November 3, 1981. Were the provinces really serious, or were they merely trying to raise a conflict of schedules that would have further postponed the meeting? Whatever that may be, the federal government was serious and despite that situation, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) scheduled a meeting for November 2 next.
In his answer to my question, the Prime Minister indicated his intention to go through with the resolution, and he referred to my personal position on the question. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a final clarification on my position which, as will be known, is different from that held by the Liberal caucus and the government. My disagreement has to do basically with Section 133. First of all the Charter of Rights is aimed at guaranteeing minorities of both official languages the essential instruments of their survival.
Theoretially, the Charter should give them protection beyond the provincial legislatures. Such is the spirit of the Charter, which has a universal thrust.
Unfortunately the Charter is affected in actual practice by other constitutional provisions, such as Section 133 of the British North America Act and Section 23 of the Manitoba Act. Under these provisions, the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba alone have been required to grant their minorities free access to the legislative and legal institutions in their own language. All the other provinces, except New Brunswick which has granted voluntarily that protection to its minority in the resolution, were exempted.
The result is that although the Charter of Rights provides legal guarantees and enshrines freedom of movement across Canada, a French-speaking citizen will never be entitled to process of law in his own language in seven provinces out of ten. He will not be able to do business, transact or contract in his own language, and so forth. This situation stems from the non-application of Section 133 all across Canada.
I would invite you, Mr. Speaker, to go through a somewhat hallucinating experience. Read the Charter again, as if you were residing in Alberta, in Ontario, or in any of the seven provinces to which Section 133 does not apply. Let us take a few examples:
10.	Everyone has the right on arrest or detention (a) to be informed promptly of the reasons therefor;
In what language, Mr. Speaker?
(b) to retain and instruct counsel without delay and to be informed of that
right;
In what language, Mr. Speaker?
And I go to Section 11:
11.	Any person charged with an offence has the right
(a)	to be informed without unreasonable delay of the specific offence;
In what language, Mr. Speaker?
(b)	to be tried within a reasonable time;
In what language, Mr. Speaker? And I could go on and on because that is the thrust of my objection. The rights granted in theory by the charter will never exist in fact, and to my mind, the resolution is incomplete in that regard.
The pan-Canadian rights of the French-speaking majority in Quebec are based on the premise that the rights of Frenchspeaking minorities outside Quebec, to which l belong, as a
mmiii
October 26, 1981

Franco-Ontarian in Ontario, be recognized. If those minorities have no real rights, that means that Quebec francophones will then have rights only in their home province. In principle their language will confine them to their province or to no more than two other Canadian provinces which, once again theoretically, should grant rights of access to judicial and legislative institutions.
I therefore wonder, Mr. Speaker, who in Canada speaks for Francophones. Is it the Quebec government or the federal government? If it is really the Quebec government, then the road to independence is already paved and through this official recognition of the French fact in America, French becomes the exclusive domain of the province of Quebec in this country. If, on the contrary, and as I believe, Mr. Speaker, it is the responsibility of the federal government, then all the provinces, without exception, should adhere to national objectives, which are to build a free and officially bilingual democratic country, which recognizes equal rights to all its citizens everywhere.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude on a more optimistic note. In spite of certain reserves, I am equally in favour of patriating our Constitution. I am equally in favour of the inclusion of a full charter of rights and freedoms. And I am equally in favour of adopting an amending formula. Unfortunately, I am unable to support the constitutional package as it stands now, because I feel the Charter is incomplete.
In view of the fact that the issues thus raised are, quite logically, significant for the future of Canada, some would like us to believe that the discussion on the whole question of the imposition of Clause 133 would be given top priority at the first federal-provincial conference following patriation. In spite of the stubborn opposition of Premier Bill Davis of Ontario, we will forge ahead.
Mr. Speaker, a Constitution essentially designed and written for a short period of time would not command the support of all Canadians. As a matter of fact, all legitimate authority derives from the Constitution. The people and other minority groups would not feel bound by such short-term arrangements.
If the constitutional rules, Mr. Speaker, must be constantly redrafted, how can we expect to develop a completely stable community? If the constitutional rules must be altered because we are convinced that their intent is deficient, the present scheme being a glaring example for the reasons I have just stated, why then postpone what can be quite properly done today?
Mr. Speaker, considering the importance of this matter and the short time at my disposal, I should like to say in conclusion that I hope to state in greater detail in the House my objection to that incomplete Charter and the reasons for my disagreement during that special two-day debate following which, 1 hope, that resolution will be forwarded abroad.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-POSSIBLE POSTPONEMENT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for having raised this very important question. [English]
I know the hon. member is aware of the Prime Minister's response to the question from the provinces as to when we are going to have a meeting. As the hon. member knows, since the Supreme Court decision came down the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) offered to the premiers of the provinces six alternative dates in which to discuss the Constitution.
The Prime Minister indicated in his telex to Premier Bennett that he was:
Prepared to meet with all the premiers one last time in an effort to reach an agreement on constitutional reform.
According to the ten premiers and the Prime Minister, pursuant to this final offer, they will be sitting down next Monday for a final round of negotiations and, as the Prime Minister said, "We will negotiate even if we have to go day and night". This House is surely aware of the proposed resolution.
In the words of the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party, we have contained in our resolution what is undoubtedly and I quote, "the best bill of rights of any country in the whole world."
Last week a public opinion poll revealed that more than 80 per cent of Canadians want a charter of rights enshrined in our Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, we are obviously on the verge of giving to the Canadian people a charter of rights which will not only protect the linguistic rights of English-speaking Quebecers, but which will also, for the first time, guarantee in the Constitution that the French-speaking minority in the nine other Canadian provinces can be educated in their own language.

Mr. Speaker, we heard the Supreme Court rule on the legality of the constitutional package. We have now obtained agreement on a final date for negotiations, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) requested last week. Let us now, in a spirit of conciliation, co-operation and good will, meet with the premiers. We want an agreement. We want that accord. We will not sacrifice fundamental principle, but we look forward to that meeting.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-MEASURES TO AID MARITIME REGION B) REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
THE ECONOMY-MEASURES TO AID MARITIME REGION B) REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak tonight about the continuing high interest rates which plague the Atlantic provinces, as they do the rest of our country, and about the particularly severe effect they are having on the economy of the Atlantic provinces. I want to

October 26, 1981
Adjournment Debate
share with the Elouse my knowledge of the situation, which I find very distressing, and I want to propose some solutions to the problem for the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) as he prepares his budget for presentation in a few weeks' time.
The latest Statistics Canada figures which have been released indicate that unemployment in our nation has increased from 7 per cent to 8.2 per cent. In every one of the Atlantic provinces this increase of 1.2 per cent has been exceeded, and in one of the Atlantic provinces the increase has been tripled.
Perhaps the most significant feature of these figures is that we have a very serious drop in employment. This means that the increase in unemployment is not because of an increase in the work force or the number of Canadians who live in the Atlantic provinces who are seeking employment. It is because we have had a cancelling out, or a drop, in the number of jobs. The Atlantic provinces are the first hit, the hardest hit and the last to recover from high interest policies and restrictive monetary policies because of the nature of their economies. Three of the Atlantic provinces have resource-based economies, and the fourth has a service-based economy.
The peculiar capital structure that is necessary for resource-based economies and service-based economies is that intense amounts of capital are required but, because of inventory and the primary nature of the products involved, very expensive working capital is required, and in the Atlantic provinces this is generally borrowed. This is where the impact of high interest policies afflicts us quite severely. The first symptoms of this affliction are the closing of our fishing plants-and they are closed-and of our lumber mills-and they are closed. The final phase is when the spin-off of these closures hits our retail merchandising establishments. Just last week two clothing stores which have been in existence for generations joined with others which have closed. This is the complexion of the problem which faces us in Atlantic Canada. I want Parliament to be aware of it, and I want the Minister of Finance to address it, particularly as he prepares his budget.
The one aspect of this problem which is perhaps most severe is the strange dichotomy of our lending institutions with record high profits and of borrowers who are losing their homes and their jobs. This is very severe, particularly for home owners, but it is also severe for tenants because some of them have seen their rents doubled and tripled as the impact has worked through our system.
The big concern I have is for Canadians in lower and middle-income groups, and I want to remind the House that in the Atlantic provinces the average income is two thirds of that in other parts of our nation. It is two thirds of the national average. People in low income groups first have to address the question of very high mortgage payments as they renew their mortgages and, next, record high heating costs, and the Atlantic provinces have the longest and most severe winters of any part of Canada. If one looks at the map, it will be seen that we
are north of Montreal. First comes the payment for the mortgage, then for home heating. If anything is left over, it goes for food. In too many families in the Atlantic provinces there is nothing left over for clothing, insurance, recreation or any of the amenities of life. Too many families are losing their homes. Too many kids are suffering from malnutrition. It is that severe. That is why I want this House to address this question.
My constituents have suggested that we consider the use of tax-free bonds for lending institutions, as do the savings companies and municipalities in the United States and the same as the electric power companies to build their works in the United States.
A lawyer in my constituency wrote suggesting that we consider rolling over the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. That has been suggested in other places. I sent this suggestion to the Minister of Finance.
Another constituent suggested that where we have record-high profits in lending institutions and record foreclosures for borrowers we consider an excess profits tax on the lending institutions, that the yield from the tax regenerate through the tax system to lower interest rates on the home owners who are renewing their mortgages.
My party proposed-and the Liberal and New Democratic parties voted against it for reasons they thought valid-a mortgage interest deductibility program. This year it would have made a maximum of $1,125 available to home owners to pay the interest on their mortgages. Next year it would have gone to $1,500.
The government has a duty to place before Parliament a proposal better than that one. If it does, I will support it. I want the government to put forward its proposal to deal constructively with the problem, and we will implement it. This should be done immediately because every day we wait, some child in the Atlantic provinces will suffer and some family will be shattered.
Finally, the government should review the high interest rate policy which, with inflation running at 12.5 per cent, is not doing the job. That is part of the problem.
We should look at the capital gains tax abolition. That abolition could act as a magnet to keep Canadian dollars at home and bring foreign dollars here through the Foreign Investment Review Act. This would strengthen the Canadian dollar and do the job that high interest rates are not doing. When you consider the cost of recovery of that tax, it is a valid point I would like the minister to address. I see, Mr. Speaker, you are about to spring from your Chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of all the
members on the other side who raise questions with the
October 26, 1981

Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) does so in the most creative fashion. I can assure him that the suggestions he has brought forward, tonight and earlier in other questions and sessions such as this, will receive very close consideration from me and from the minister as he reaches the final phase of his budget preparation.
The hon. member implied tonight that the drop in employment in the Atlantic provinces has, in some way, been greater or that the Atlantic provinces are more adversely affected by the current economic malaise that we face than perhaps other parts of the country. I suggest that equally adverse impacts are being felt across this country. The minister is considering those very seriously in his final preparations for his budget. Of course, it would be premature at this time to indicate any of the measures the minister is considering, or which the minister has already indicated he intends to adopt. However, I can assure the hon. member that a reduction in inflation and interest rates will benefit all regions and sectors of the economy. In the short run, Mr. Speaker, the high interest rates in the United States and the need in Canada to combat these inflationary expectations and keep prudent limits on the money supply growth mean, of course, that interest rates must remain relatively high across all the country. Moreover, there is no conclusive evidence that the less prosperous regions of the country are relatively harder hit by high interest rates than are the other regions.
Adjournment Debate
There are, however, continuing measures in place to assist the less advantaged regions of the country, such as, for example, expenditures by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, equalization payments, and the regionally-differentiated investment tax credits, as well the small business development bonds and other measures which, in some cases, help all of Canada, but which in many cases are strictly and closely directed towards the less advantaged regions of the country.
The hon. member has suggested there has been a dramatic increase in unemployment and a drop in employment in the maritimes at this point in time specifically. I would point out to him that from 1978 to 1980 the employment growth in the maritimes was higher than in the rest of Canada. For example, it was 4.1 per cent during that period, which exceeded the average for Canada as a whole, which was only 3.4 per cent. The latter part of the 1970s was a period of high employment growth in the maritimes and high economic investment. We hope that situation will return after we have passed this brief period of difficulty that we are facing at this time.
